models.title: Bend a path around the Moon
models.brief: Change a tangential starting speed, then follow an orbit through equal intervals of time.
assumptions: A planar Newtonian two-body model with spherical bodies. No atmosphere, terrain, thrust after the initial state, solar gravity, tides, or uneven lunar gravity. It is not an Earth-to-Moon flight planner.
Moon mode treats the spacecraft mass as negligible and uses GM = 4902.800118 km³/s² and mean lunar radius 1737.4 km. Altitude is measured above this spherical surface.

Earth–Moon mode shows the relative separation vector, using the sum of their gravitational parameters. Earth is drawn as the coordinate origin; both bodies actually move about their barycenter. Contact occurs when their mean spheres meet.

An ellipse that intersects the surface is a collision trajectory, not a usable orbit. The displayed flight stops at first contact. Open paths show a finite time window; very long bound orbits may show only part of their period.

Equal-time dots and the moving marker use Kepler time equations. Axes share one geometric scale. Velocity and gravity arrow lengths are rescaled for readability; their directions are physical. The moving marker is enlarged and does not represent the moving body’s size.

models.title: Spend fuel to change velocity
models.brief: Follow mass, speed and acceleration during an ideal deep-space engine burn.
assumptions: One straight burn starts from rest in the chosen frame. Dry mass stays positive; propellant is expelled at a constant mass rate and constant effective exhaust speed.
Gravity, drag, steering, staging, engine transients and relativity are excluded. The result is ideal delta-v capability, not a launch height or a flight plan.
At 100% burn, the acceleration readout is the limit just before engine shutoff. With no propellant there is no burn and acceleration is zero.
Mass uses kilograms, time seconds, speed meters per second and distance meters. This differs from the orbit model, which uses kilometers.

models.title: Pack a lunar outpost
models.brief: Turn a crew plan into a water manifest with whole tanks and enough capacity.
assumptions: These are invented planning quantities, not astronaut water requirements. There is no recycling, reserve margin, leakage or change in daily use.
Every tank has 5 liters of usable capacity. Fractional liters are allowed; tanks must be whole objects. Unused capacity is not unused water.
The same daily amount is assigned to every crew member. Varying individual needs would require a sum of separate amounts.

models.title: Design a game sound
models.brief: Mix two sine waves and connect phase, harmonics and signal energy to the shape you create.
assumptions: The second frequency is an integer harmonic of the first. Signals add linearly without clipping, propagation delay, room reflections or speaker distortion.
Vertical amplitude is a relative signal value, not measured sound pressure or perceived loudness. RMS is computed over a full base period.
The plotted time axis shows two base periods and changes when frequency changes. The equal-frequency case is allowed so destructive interference can be tested.

models.title: Build a game portal
models.brief: Transform a ship sprite while deciding which geometric features the portal should preserve.
assumptions: This is a two-dimensional affine transformation: scale x and y, rotate counterclockwise, then translate horizontally. It is not a three-dimensional perspective camera.
Both axes use equal units. Negative scale reflects an axis; zero scale loses a dimension. Translation changes position but not lengths or area.
The determinant describes oriented area scaling of the linear part. A nonzero horizontal translation means the full map is affine, not linear.

models.title: Power a solar music stage
models.brief: Balance daylight production, a constant electrical load and finite battery storage.
assumptions: This synthetic Earth-style day has daylight from 06:00 to 18:00. Solar power follows a sine arch; it is not a weather forecast or a model of lunar daylight.
Power uses kW; stored, spilled and unmet energy use kWh. The battery begins half full at midnight. Charging and discharging are ideal, without losses or power limits.
Solar energy is integrated exactly on each half-minute interval. Battery dispatch uses those intervals, so crossings of a full or empty battery have small time-step error.
Unserved energy means the chosen load could not be supplied at that time. Surplus energy later in the day does not retroactively serve an earlier shortage.

models.title: Send a message across the Moon
models.brief: Compare relay routes, latency and delivery probability before choosing a communication plan.
assumptions: This invented undirected network has fixed nonnegative edge delays. Diagram lengths are not physical distances. Antenna geometry, terrain and line of sight are not modeled.
A route visits each relay at most once. The model enumerates simple routes and highlights a minimum-delay choice; several routes can tie.
Each edge independently fails for each packet with the same chosen probability. No retries or backup routing occur. A route with k edges succeeds with probability (1−p)^k.
Expected delivered packets is a mean over hypothetical repeats, not a guaranteed count. Delivery events on alternate routes sharing edges are not automatically independent.

missions.title: Count the cargo before the hatch closes
missions.brief: A manifest has to count actual tanks, not just marks on a screen.
missions.connection: A manifest has to count actual tanks, not just marks on a screen.
missions.prediction: With one person, one day and 2.5 L each, will one tank be enough?
missions.manipulate: Set that plan, then count the whole tanks as you add crew one person at a time.
missions.decision: Write a tank list for three people over four days. How do you know no tank was counted twice?
missions.clue: Pair each tank symbol with exactly one number. The last number is the count.

missions.title: Read the manifest without losing a zero
missions.brief: A misplaced digit can turn a small water order into a much larger load.
missions.connection: A misplaced digit can turn a small water order into a much larger load.
missions.prediction: How different are 12 L and 120 L, even though the same nonzero digits appear?
missions.manipulate: Use three people at 4 L each for one day and then ten days. Read 12 L and 120 L aloud and compare the tank counts.
missions.decision: Expand each total using tens, ones and tenths. Explain what would change if its decimal point moved.
missions.clue: A digit's value depends on its position; keep liters attached to the whole number.

missions.title: Use the last tank wisely
missions.brief: The gap between packed capacity and required water is a subtraction problem with meaning.
missions.connection: The gap between packed capacity and required water is a subtraction problem with meaning.
missions.prediction: If you need 27 L and five tanks hold 25 L, what is missing?
missions.manipulate: Try three people, three days and 3 L per person; compare required water and packed capacity.
missions.decision: Explain how adding one tank changes both capacity and the remaining gap. Distinguish extra capacity from extra water.
missions.clue: Write capacity minus requirement, then interpret the sign before deciding what to pack.

missions.title: Build a crew-by-day water plan
missions.brief: Equal groups connect people, days, water and tank capacity.
missions.connection: Equal groups connect people, days, water and tank capacity.
missions.prediction: Will doubling both crew and days double the water, or change it another way?
missions.manipulate: Compare two crew for three days with four crew for six days at the same daily rate.
missions.decision: Show the repeated groups first, then use multiplication. Divide by tank capacity and explain any rounding.
missions.clue: Crew × days counts person-days. Each person-day uses the same number of liters.

missions.title: Check a disputed cargo formula
missions.brief: The order of operations decides whether a formula matches the actual packing story.
missions.connection: The order of operations decides whether a formula matches the actual packing story.
missions.prediction: Which represents three crew using 2 L daily for four days: 3×2×4 or 3×(2+4)?
missions.manipulate: Set the first plan and compare the model with both calculations.
missions.decision: Invent a plan with an additional 5 L shared reserve. Write one expression and explain its grouping.
missions.clue: Do the crew's repeated daily use first; add the shared reserve once, not once per person.

missions.title: Make a quick loading estimate
missions.brief: Before exact packing, a rough bound catches an implausible manifest.
missions.connection: Before exact packing, a rough bound catches an implausible manifest.
missions.prediction: Is water for seven people over nine days at 2.5 L closer to 15 L, 150 L or 1500 L?
missions.manipulate: Estimate first, then set the values and inspect the exact total.
missions.decision: Give a lower and upper estimate using nearby easy numbers. Explain whether a 5-tank order is plausible.
missions.clue: Use units and easy products such as 7×10×2 or 7×10×3 before exact arithmetic.

missions.title: Share the tank, not the mistake
missions.brief: Fractional daily amounts can still lead to a whole-number packing decision.
missions.connection: Fractional daily amounts can still lead to a whole-number packing decision.
missions.prediction: Three people use 2½ L each in one day. How much of a 5 L tank is that total?
missions.manipulate: Set that plan and then extend it to three days.
missions.decision: Represent the liters as improper fractions, multiply, and explain why tank count must be rounded upward.
missions.clue: Convert mixed numbers before multiplying. Rounding a tank count downward can leave water without a container.

missions.title: Read the quarter-liter marks
missions.brief: A decimal describes an amount, while a tank count describes objects.
missions.connection: A decimal describes an amount, while a tank count describes objects.
missions.prediction: Is 0.75 L three times 0.25 L? Predict the total for five people.
missions.manipulate: Compare daily rates 0.75 and 1.25 L for the same crew and days.
missions.decision: Explain the difference using hundredths or quarters, then check your decimal subtraction.
missions.clue: Align place values when subtracting; a trailing zero does not change the amount.

missions.title: Audit the fuel gauge
missions.brief: A fuel gauge measures a fraction of propellant, not a fraction of all rocket mass.
missions.connection: A fuel gauge measures a fraction of propellant, not a fraction of all rocket mass.
missions.prediction: At 50% burn, has the rocket lost half its total initial mass?
missions.manipulate: Compare a rocket with 2000 kg dry mass and 6000 kg propellant at 0%, 50% and 100%.
missions.decision: Report the percentage of propellant used and the percentage of initial total mass lost. Explain why they differ.
missions.clue: Name the denominator of each percentage: propellant initially, or all initial mass.

missions.title: Compare two fuel-heavy designs
missions.brief: The ratio of full mass to dry mass matters more than fuel mass alone.
missions.connection: The ratio of full mass to dry mass matters more than fuel mass alone.
missions.prediction: Will two rockets with the same full-to-dry mass ratio have the same ideal delta-v at the same exhaust speed?
missions.manipulate: Compare 1000 kg dry plus 3000 kg propellant with 2000 kg dry plus 6000 kg propellant.
missions.decision: State which quantities scale together and which output stays the same. Explain why burn time may still differ.
missions.clue: Write each mass ratio before comparing; equal ratios do not mean equal total mass.

missions.title: Resize an outpost without changing the plan
missions.brief: Keeping liters per person per day fixed is a proportional model.
missions.connection: Keeping liters per person per day fixed is a proportional model.
missions.prediction: If a six-person plan uses a given total, should a two-person plan use one third as much?
missions.manipulate: Hold days and daily rate fixed; compare crew sizes two, four and six.
missions.decision: Create a proportion relating people and liters, then name one real condition that could break it.
missions.clue: A shared reserve or a fixed setup cost would add a term that does not scale with crew.

missions.title: Explain an energy deficit
missions.brief: A negative net energy means consumption exceeds production during an interval.
missions.connection: A negative net energy means consumption exceeds production during an interval.
missions.prediction: At midnight with positive load, is production minus demand positive or negative?
missions.manipulate: Compare the night and noon portions of the day; reduce battery size to expose a shortage.
missions.decision: Describe what a negative balance means physically without calling it negative electricity stored in the battery.
missions.clue: Stored energy is clamped at zero. The unsupplied demand is tracked separately.

missions.title: Scale an orbit beyond intuition
missions.brief: For a circular orbit, radius powers connect distance and travel time.
missions.connection: For a circular orbit, radius powers connect distance and travel time.
missions.prediction: If orbital radius becomes four times as large, does the period become four times as long?
missions.manipulate: Use circular presets at two starting altitudes; record their center distances and periods.
missions.decision: Use T² proportional to r³ to predict a period ratio. Explain why altitude alone cannot be substituted for r.
missions.clue: Radius is surface radius plus altitude. Powers act on the full center distance.

missions.title: Find the speed that closes the circle
missions.brief: Circular speed comes from the positive square root of gravitational parameter divided by radius.
missions.connection: Circular speed comes from the positive square root of gravitational parameter divided by radius.
missions.prediction: When center distance increases, should circular speed increase or decrease?
missions.manipulate: At two altitudes, choose Circular and compare the displayed speeds.
missions.decision: Use v=√(μ/r) and check the squared result. Explain why this speed uses the positive root.
missions.clue: Squaring tests the formula; speed is a magnitude and cannot be negative.

missions.title: Name every part of a cargo plan
missions.brief: Variables let one water rule serve many crews instead of one fixed answer.
missions.connection: Variables let one water rule serve many crews instead of one fixed answer.
missions.prediction: Which input would you call c, d and w in a crew plan?
missions.manipulate: Change only one of crew, days or liters per person and watch the total.
missions.decision: Write W=cdw and define every variable with units. Identify the output separately from its inputs.
missions.clue: A variable is a named quantity; it is not automatically something you must solve for.

missions.title: Split the crew without changing the total
missions.brief: Distribution explains why two subteams' supplies can equal the whole team's plan.
missions.connection: Distribution explains why two subteams' supplies can equal the whole team's plan.
missions.prediction: For 2 scouts and 3 builders, will (2+3)×4×2.5 equal two separately packed amounts?
missions.manipulate: Compare the five-person plan with a two-person and a three-person plan using the same days and rate.
missions.decision: Expand the grouped expression and name the shared factor. Explain why adding tank counts can differ from packing together.
missions.clue: Liters add exactly. Separately rounding each team's tank count can add spare capacity.

missions.title: Find the missing crew size
missions.brief: An unknown input can be recovered from a known total when the other factors are fixed.
missions.connection: An unknown input can be recovered from a known total when the other factors are fixed.
missions.prediction: A one-day plan uses 15 L at 2.5 L per person. How many people is it for?
missions.manipulate: Set the daily rate, solve before moving crew, then verify with the model.
missions.decision: Write and solve one equation, naming the inverse operation and the unit of your answer.
missions.clue: Divide total liters by liters per person; the liter units cancel.

missions.title: Account for a shared emergency reserve
missions.brief: A plan with a fixed reserve needs more than one inverse operation.
missions.connection: A plan with a fixed reserve needs more than one inverse operation.
missions.prediction: If 4 days at 2 L per person plus a 5 L shared reserve totals 45 L, what is the crew size?
missions.manipulate: Use the model for the daily portion, then add the fixed reserve on paper.
missions.decision: Explain why you subtract the reserve before dividing, and check the original equation.
missions.clue: Keep the model's no-reserve output separate from the extra 5 L in this task.

missions.title: Stay within the tank limit
missions.brief: A capacity constraint usually allows a range of plans, not one equality.
missions.connection: A capacity constraint usually allows a range of plans, not one equality.
missions.prediction: With six 5 L tanks, can four people stay four days at 2 L per day?
missions.manipulate: Adjust days and crew to find plans just below and just above 30 L.
missions.decision: Write a capacity inequality and describe every whole-number day count allowed for a chosen crew.
missions.clue: Treat days as positive integers. A fractional algebraic bound must be interpreted before planning.

missions.title: Place a game ship on the map
missions.brief: A point needs both horizontal and vertical coordinates to specify its location.
missions.connection: A point needs both horizontal and vertical coordinates to specify its location.
missions.prediction: What happens to the ship when only horizontal pan changes?
missions.manipulate: Keep scales at 1 and angle at 0; move the pan left and right.
missions.decision: Record the nose coordinates before and after a shift. Explain which coordinate stayed fixed.
missions.clue: Translation adds a displacement to position; it does not multiply both coordinates.

missions.title: Read a rocket as an input-output rule
missions.brief: Time is an input to the rocket's mass, velocity and distance functions.
missions.connection: Time is an input to the rocket's mass, velocity and distance functions.
missions.prediction: Can the same time have two velocities in this fixed model?
missions.manipulate: Choose one rocket, move burn progress and record three time–velocity pairs.
missions.decision: Explain how changing the rocket's fuel creates a different function, rather than another output for the same fixed input.
missions.clue: A function includes its fixed parameters and its allowed input interval.

missions.title: Turn an outpost message into mathematics
missions.brief: The story must specify who uses what, for how long and what is being counted.
missions.connection: The story must specify who uses what, for how long and what is being counted.
missions.prediction: Which information is missing from “pack enough water for a crew”?
missions.manipulate: Choose a complete plan and inspect liters and whole tanks separately.
missions.decision: Write a short packing recommendation with a formula, numerical result, units and one stated assumption.
missions.clue: Underline quantities and units first. Decide whether the requested answer is water amount or container count.

missions.title: Price a water delivery
missions.brief: A fixed delivery fee plus a per-liter charge creates a straight-line cost model.
missions.connection: A fixed delivery fee plus a per-liter charge creates a straight-line cost model.
missions.prediction: For an invented $12 fixed fee plus $3 per liter, what does the cost equal when no water is ordered?
missions.manipulate: Use supply totals as order quantities, then calculate costs for three different quantities.
missions.decision: Write C=12+3L and solve the order size for a chosen budget. Explain the intercept and slope.
missions.clue: The supply display gives L; the cost calculation is a separate extension using dollars.

missions.title: Choose a feasible constant load
missions.brief: A daily energy budget creates a necessary inequality, but timing still matters.
missions.connection: A daily energy budget creates a necessary inequality, but timing still matters.
missions.prediction: If daily demand exceeds generated energy plus initial storage, can the whole day be supplied?
missions.manipulate: Try loads above and below that daily bound while holding panels and battery fixed.
missions.decision: Derive 24L≤generated+initial as a necessary condition, then explain why it alone does not guarantee no shortage.
missions.clue: A daily total ignores when the battery becomes empty or full.

missions.title: Decode a two-module manifest
missions.brief: Two independent totals can identify two unknown quantities.
missions.connection: Two independent totals can identify two unknown quantities.
missions.prediction: A scout uses 2 L daily and a builder 3 L. If six people use 16 L, how many are each type?
missions.manipulate: Use equal-rate plans to check each group's proposed contribution separately.
missions.decision: Write the person-count and water-count equations, solve them together and verify both totals.
missions.clue: One equation counts people; the other weights people by different water rates.

missions.title: Treat a waveform as a rule
missions.brief: A sound signal assigns an amplitude to every time within its domain.
missions.connection: A sound signal assigns an amplitude to every time within its domain.
missions.prediction: If phase changes, is the input time changing or the function changing?
missions.manipulate: Hold frequency fixed and compare two phases at the same horizontal position.
missions.decision: Describe the input, output and parameters. Explain why a vertical waveform point is not the sound's position in space.
missions.clue: This plot is amplitude versus time at one location, not a picture of a moving object.

missions.title: Compare average speed gain
missions.brief: The slope of a velocity graph measures acceleration over a chosen interval.
missions.connection: The slope of a velocity graph measures acceleration over a chosen interval.
missions.prediction: During a constant-flow burn, will equal time intervals add equal amounts of velocity?
missions.manipulate: Compare early and late equal fractions of the same burn.
missions.decision: Calculate two average slopes Δv/Δt with units. Explain why the lighter rocket can have a larger slope.
missions.clue: Read differences of outputs and inputs; the coordinate v/t is not generally an interval slope.

missions.title: Tell the story of a day from a graph
missions.brief: Power and stored energy answer different questions even when they share a time axis.
missions.connection: Power and stored energy answer different questions even when they share a time axis.
missions.prediction: Can the battery still be charging after solar power has begun falling?
missions.manipulate: Move panel peak and battery capacity; compare the power and storage curves.
missions.decision: Describe an increasing, flat and decreasing part of storage using production minus load.
missions.clue: Storage increases when power exceeds load, until capacity is reached.

missions.title: Account for every part of an area change
missions.brief: Expanding a product explains a game portal’s combined horizontal and vertical area scale.
missions.connection: Expanding a product explains a game portal’s combined horizontal and vertical area scale.
missions.prediction: Does (x+1)(x+2) contain only x² and 2, or do cross terms also change the area?
missions.manipulate: Set angle and pan to zero. For x=0, 0.2 and 0.5, set horizontal scale x+1 and vertical scale x+2.
missions.decision: Expand the product and compare it with the displayed area multiplier. Explain what each cross term represents in a rectangular area diagram.
missions.clue: Each term from one scale factor multiplies each term from the other. The multiplier applies to the whole sprite’s original area.

missions.title: Recover the dimensions from the area
missions.brief: Factoring can turn a screen-area expression into usable dimensions.
missions.connection: Factoring can turn a screen-area expression into usable dimensions.
missions.prediction: Which positive scale factors could produce the area multiplier x²+3x+2?
missions.manipulate: Compare your factors at x=0 and x=0.5 with the portal’s horizontal and vertical scale controls.
missions.decision: Factor the polynomial, verify its area multiplier and state the x values for which both chosen scale factors are positive.
missions.clue: Find two numbers with sum 3 and product 2. Positivity is an additional design restriction on the factors.

missions.title: Design a rectangular habitat floor
missions.brief: A fixed wall budget makes usable area a quadratic in one side length.
missions.connection: A fixed wall budget makes usable area a quadratic in one side length.
missions.prediction: With 20 m of wall, would a long thin floor or a square give more area?
missions.manipulate: Draw a grid beside the supply plan; compare widths 1, 3 and 5 with length 10−w.
missions.decision: Build A(w)=w(10−w), locate its largest value and explain the allowed interval. Connect area to how many crew stations fit.
missions.clue: This is a design extension; the tank model does not calculate floor area. Complete the square or compare symmetric widths.

missions.title: See reliability shrink over more relays
missions.brief: Independent per-edge survival multiplies along a route.
missions.connection: Independent per-edge survival multiplies along a route.
missions.prediction: At 10% failure per edge, is a three-edge route's success probability 70% or something else?
missions.manipulate: Change edge failure and compare routes with different hop counts.
missions.decision: Write S(k)=(1−p)^k and explain its starting value and repeated multiplier.
missions.clue: Subtracting p once per hop ignores the changing group of packets still alive.

missions.title: Turn the ship through a checkpoint
missions.brief: Rotation gives angles an immediate consequence for a sprite's direction.
missions.connection: Rotation gives angles an immediate consequence for a sprite's direction.
missions.prediction: Where will the nose point after a positive quarter turn from zero rotation?
missions.manipulate: Set both scales to 1 and pan to 0; try 0°, 90°, 180° and −90°.
missions.decision: Describe clockwise and counterclockwise turns and the equivalence of a full turn.
missions.clue: Positive angles rotate counterclockwise in the mathematical coordinate system.

missions.title: Keep the ship’s triangular frame in proportion
missions.brief: The nose and two outer wing tips define a triangle whose side and angle relationships expose a portal’s distortion.
missions.connection: The nose and two outer wing tips define a triangle whose side and angle relationships expose a portal’s distortion.
missions.prediction: Will stretching only horizontally preserve the angles of the triangle joining the nose and outer wing tips?
missions.manipulate: Use vertices (0,1.3), (−0.8,−0.7) and (0.8,−0.7). Compare a uniform scale with a horizontal-only scale, keeping rotation and translation zero.
missions.decision: Calculate two side ratios and decide whether the resulting triangles are similar.
missions.clue: Equal scaling in every direction preserves angles; nonuniform scaling generally does not.

missions.title: Teleport without resizing
missions.brief: A congruent sprite can move and turn while keeping every distance.
missions.connection: A congruent sprite can move and turn while keeping every distance.
missions.prediction: Does translating a ship change the distances between its vertices?
missions.manipulate: Use unit scales, vary angle and pan, and compare the shape.
missions.decision: Give a coordinate argument that rotation and translation preserve a selected side length.
missions.clue: Subtract endpoint coordinates before measuring a side; translation cancels from that difference.

missions.title: Make a miniature ship that still looks right
missions.brief: A uniform scale preserves shape while changing all lengths by one factor.
missions.connection: A uniform scale preserves shape while changing all lengths by one factor.
missions.prediction: If lengths double, will area double or quadruple?
missions.manipulate: Compare scales (1,1), (2,2) and (2,1).
missions.decision: Choose which pair of images is similar and justify with both length ratios and area scale.
missions.clue: Area combines two independent length dimensions.

missions.title: Compare a circular patrol with an ellipse
missions.brief: A circular orbit keeps its center distance fixed even while velocity turns.
missions.connection: A circular orbit keeps its center distance fixed even while velocity turns.
missions.prediction: Will equal-time dots be equally spaced around a circular path?
missions.manipulate: Choose Circular, then change the speed slightly while keeping altitude fixed.
missions.decision: Explain the change in radius and dot spacing; distinguish circle radius from altitude above the Moon.
missions.clue: A circle is the eccentricity-zero member of the ellipse family.

missions.title: Use area under a power curve
missions.brief: A region on a power-versus-time graph represents an amount of energy.
missions.connection: A region on a power-versus-time graph represents an amount of energy.
missions.prediction: Do two hours at 2 kW and one hour at 4 kW produce the same energy?
missions.manipulate: Compare rectangular estimates of the solar arch with the generated-energy readout.
missions.decision: Label horizontal and vertical units and explain why their product is kWh.
missions.clue: The geometric area has a physical interpretation only after both axis units are identified.

missions.title: Give the tanks real dimensions
missions.brief: Water capacity is volume; surface area instead measures the material around it.
missions.connection: Water capacity is volume; surface area instead measures the material around it.
missions.prediction: Would doubling every tank dimension double its capacity?
missions.manipulate: Relate a 5 L tank to 5000 cm³, then compare a uniformly doubled design.
missions.decision: Propose a rectangular tank with that volume and calculate its surface area separately.
missions.clue: 1 L=1000 cm³. Three length factors determine volume, while two determine surface area.

missions.title: Locate both foci of an orbital ellipse
missions.brief: The Moon sits at a focus, not generally at the ellipse's center.
missions.connection: The Moon sits at a focus, not generally at the ellipse's center.
missions.prediction: Will the ellipse's center stay at the Moon after you raise starting speed?
missions.manipulate: Choose a clearly elliptical non-colliding path and record nearest and farthest distance.
missions.decision: Use a=(rnear+rfar)/2 and c=(rfar−rnear)/2 to locate the center and other focus.
missions.clue: The difference between the near and far distances reveals how far the focus is from the center.

missions.title: Prove a portal preserves distance
missions.brief: A few matching pictures suggest a property; a proof must handle arbitrary points.
missions.connection: A few matching pictures suggest a property; a proof must handle arbitrary points.
missions.prediction: Does testing one side prove that every length is preserved?
missions.manipulate: Use unit scales and a rotation, then test another side to form a conjecture.
missions.decision: For a displacement (u,v), show the rotated squared length is u²+v². State the identity you use.
missions.clue: Expand both squares; the cross terms cancel and sin²θ+cos²θ=1.

missions.title: Summarize route delays honestly
missions.brief: Mean, median and minimum route delay describe different aspects of the same list.
missions.connection: Mean, median and minimum route delay describe different aspects of the same list.
missions.prediction: Will the fastest route necessarily be close to the mean route delay?
missions.manipulate: List the simple-route costs at one setting and compute their mean and median.
missions.decision: Recommend which summary answers “fastest possible” and which describes a typical listed route. State that routes are not equally likely unless chosen that way.
missions.clue: A numerical average needs a clearly defined collection and weighting.

missions.title: Measure how uneven the route options are
missions.brief: Squared deviations quantify spread around an average delay.
missions.connection: Squared deviations quantify spread around an average delay.
missions.prediction: Can two networks have the same mean delay but different spread?
missions.manipulate: Change ridge and crater delays; write down two route-cost lists.
missions.decision: Compute population variance for the full displayed list and explain its squared units.
missions.clue: Subtract the list mean, square each deviation, then average. This is not yet a sample-based estimate.

missions.title: Return spread to milliseconds
missions.brief: Taking the square root brings variance back to a delay unit.
missions.connection: Taking the square root brings variance back to a delay unit.
missions.prediction: If every delay were multiplied by 2, how would standard deviation change?
missions.manipulate: Record one complete route list and a hypothetical doubled list.
missions.decision: Compare variance and standard deviation, then explain why milliseconds are easier to interpret than ms².
missions.clue: Variance scales by the square of a scale factor; standard deviation scales by its absolute value.

missions.title: Look beyond the average relay delay
missions.brief: A distribution preserves information that a single summary can hide.
missions.connection: A distribution preserves information that a single summary can hide.
missions.prediction: Could many routes be fast while a few very long routes pull up the mean?
missions.manipulate: Sort or sketch a dot plot of all route delays and then raise one edge delay.
missions.decision: Describe which routes move together and why the shape changes.
missions.clue: Routes share edges, so changing one edge can move several observations at once.

missions.title: Question a tempting network pattern
missions.brief: Routes with more hops can correlate with longer delay without hop count determining delay alone.
missions.connection: Routes with more hops can correlate with longer delay without hop count determining delay alone.
missions.prediction: Must every three-hop route be slower than every two-hop route?

missions.title: Understand the steepening acceleration

missions.title: Rotate with a complex multiplier

missions.title: Plan for a chain of relays

missions.title: Ask what more fuel really buys

missions.title: Track delivery through successive hops

missions.title: Budget several ideal burns

missions.title: Resolve the ship's direction
missions.brief: A rotated unit direction has horizontal and vertical components.
missions.connection: A rotated unit direction has horizontal and vertical components.
missions.prediction: At a 30° turn, which component of a unit horizontal arrow is larger?
missions.manipulate: Keep scales at 1 and pan at 0; compare 30°, 45° and 60°.
missions.decision: Draw the right triangle and recover each component using the correct sine or cosine ratio.

missions.title: Point the velocity arrow correctly
missions.brief: An orbital velocity has two components, and their ratio can describe its direction.

missions.prediction: Is the velocity arrow radial or tangent on a circular orbit?
missions.manipulate: Choose Circular and move through a quarter of the time window.

missions.title: Turn one direction through every quadrant
missions.brief: The unit circle organizes a rotation's cosine and sine components.

missions.prediction: What signs should the image of (1,0) have after 120°?

missions.title: Convert a phase knob into a formula
missions.brief: Sine functions in calculus use radian phase even when a control is labeled in degrees.

missions.title: Make a brighter game tone
missions.brief: Harmonics change the waveform's shape while the base frequency sets its repeat window.

missions.title: Explain silence from two active waves
missions.brief: An identity explains why two signals can cancel at every time.
missions.connection: An identity explains why two signals can cancel at every time.
missions.prediction: Can two nonzero equal-frequency signals sum to zero everywhere?
missions.manipulate: Set harmonic 1, mix 1 and phase 180°, then try a different phase.

missions.title: Find when the panels meet the load
missions.brief: A sine equation identifies the times when production changes from below to above demand.
missions.connection: A sine equation identifies the times when production changes from below to above demand.

missions.title: Shift a sound without redrawing it
missions.brief: Phase, amplitude and frequency transform a base sine graph in different ways.

missions.clue: For sin(ωt+φ), solve ωt+φ=0 to locate the shifted phase origin.

missions.title: Follow time through mass into speed
missions.brief: A rocket's speed formula is a chain of functions: time changes mass, then the mass ratio changes velocity.
missions.connection: A rocket's speed formula is a chain of functions: time changes mass, then the mass ratio changes velocity.
missions.prediction: If time increases, which intermediate quantity decreases?
missions.manipulate: Choose a burn point and calculate t→m0−qt→m0/m→ve ln(m0/m).
missions.decision: Explain each arrow's meaning and domain. Describe how an error in the mass step affects the final speed.
missions.clue: The logarithm receives a positive dimensionless ratio, not a mass carrying units.

missions.title: Work backward from a target speed
missions.brief: An inverse answers when an ideal burn reaches a chosen velocity gain.
missions.connection: An inverse answers when an ideal burn reaches a chosen velocity gain.
missions.prediction: Is every positive target delta-v reachable before the fuel runs out?
missions.manipulate: Choose a target below the displayed maximum and estimate the matching progress.
missions.decision: Solve t=(m0/q)(1−exp(−v/ve)), then check that it lies within the allowed burn.
missions.clue: An algebraic inverse still needs the original function's output range.

missions.title: Compare an expensive extra kilometer per second
missions.brief: Inverting a logarithmic gain exposes exponential mass requirements.
missions.connection: Inverting a logarithmic gain exposes exponential mass requirements.
missions.prediction: Does adding the same delta-v always require adding the same amount of propellant?
missions.manipulate: At fixed dry mass and exhaust speed, compare mass ratios for two equally spaced velocity targets.
missions.decision: Derive m0/mf=exp(Δv/ve) and explain why multiplying ratios is different from adding fuel.
missions.clue: The exponent must be dimensionless; use consistent speed units.

missions.title: Move a dot around an oval
missions.brief: One clock controls two coordinates, like a camera following a track.
missions.connection: One clock controls two coordinates, like a camera following a track.
missions.prediction: Where will the dot be after a quarter of a lap?
missions.manipulate: Move the time slider, then stretch the track.
missions.decision: Use the two coordinate rules to predict the dot’s position after half a lap.
missions.clue: A quarter lap reaches the top. A half lap reaches the left side.

missions.title: Describe an orbit from its focus
missions.brief: Polar coordinates measure radius from the attracting body, a natural origin for a conic.
missions.connection: Polar coordinates measure radius from the attracting body, a natural origin for a conic.
missions.prediction: Will an ellipse have a constant polar radius?
missions.manipulate: Choose an elliptical orbit and compare near and far positions.
missions.decision: Use r=p/(1+e cosθ), with θ measured from periapsis, to recover near and far radii.
missions.clue: The sign and reference direction of θ matter. The focus is not the ellipse center.

missions.title: Build a richer tone one harmonic at a time
missions.brief: A sum of sinusoidal components is the beginning of a Fourier description.
missions.connection: A sum of sinusoidal components is the beginning of a Fourier description.
missions.prediction: Could a sharp-edged waveform be reproduced exactly by only two smooth sine waves?
missions.manipulate: Compare the two-component model with a paper sketch adding a third and fifth harmonic.
missions.decision: Propose a sequence of partial sums and explain what sense of approximation you would measure.
missions.clue: Two harmonics illustrate superposition; a full Fourier-series experiment needs more components and a stated error norm.

missions.title: Zoom into one instant of a burn
missions.brief: Average acceleration over shorter intervals suggests an instantaneous rate.
missions.connection: Average acceleration over shorter intervals suggests an instantaneous rate.
missions.prediction: Should early and late shrinking intervals approach the same acceleration in this burn?
missions.manipulate: Choose a middle time and estimate velocity change over progressively smaller intervals.
missions.decision: Describe the limiting quotient and distinguish the limit from setting its denominator to zero.
missions.clue: Both numerator and denominator shrink; their ratio can approach a finite value.

missions.title: Find the acceleration hiding between readings
missions.brief: A rocket speed table gives average changes; the engine responds at each instant.
missions.connection: The ideal burn has v(t) = ve ln(m0/(m0 - qt)), with positive remaining mass. A difference quotient compares two times; its limit describes acceleration at one time.
missions.prediction: Near the middle of the burn, will a short-time average acceleration agree more closely with the instantaneous readout than a long-time average?
missions.manipulate: Use dry mass 2000 kg, propellant 6000 kg, flow 100 kg/s and exhaust speed 3000 m/s. Compare speeds at 40% and 60%, then at 49% and 51%. Convert each progress difference to seconds.
missions.decision: Calculate both centered average accelerations and compare them with the 50% acceleration. Explain what the shrinking interval suggests and what the formula must establish beyond these finite readings.
missions.clue: Divide a change in speed by a nonzero change in time. Take the limit only after expressing how that quotient depends on the time interval.

missions.title: Locate the jump in a water order
missions.brief: The amount of water varies smoothly, but a supplier sells only whole tanks.
missions.connection: For two crew over two days, water W = 4r liters when r is the daily liters per person. The order is N = ceil(W/5) five-liter tanks.
missions.prediction: As r passes 2.5 liters per person per day, which output changes continuously: water needed or whole tanks ordered?
missions.manipulate: Set crew 2 and days 2. Compare r = 2.25, 2.5 and 2.75. On paper, consider values arbitrarily close to 2.5 from each side, beyond the slider step size.
missions.decision: State the function value and both one-sided limits for each output at r = 2.5. Decide which output can be safely interpolated across that threshold.
missions.clue: Continuity requires both one-sided limits to equal the function value. A full tank already meets its exact capacity; the next tank is needed immediately after that threshold.

missions.title: Explain why the burn curve gets steeper
missions.brief: A constant propellant flow does not produce constant acceleration.
missions.connection: The speed curve is v(t) = ve ln(m0/(m0 - qt)). Its slope is a rate in meters per second per second; the horizontal variable is time, not the progress percentage.
missions.prediction: With flow fixed, will acceleration be larger early or late in the burn? Identify which changing quantity could explain your prediction.
missions.manipulate: Use the default 2000 kg dry mass, 6000 kg propellant, 100 kg/s flow and 3000 m/s exhaust speed. Record mass, speed and acceleration at 25%, 50% and 75%; compare equal-time speed gains early and late.
missions.decision: Differentiate v(t), explain the sign and units, and connect the changing slope to remaining mass. Decide whether one constant acceleration can describe the entire burn accurately.
missions.clue: Write remaining mass as m0 - qt. Increasing time decreases its denominator in the acceleration expression; equal progress steps correspond to equal time steps for a fixed burn.

missions.title: Track energy when both mass and speed change
missions.brief: To analyze the remaining rocket, account for its changing mass as well as its changing speed.
missions.connection: The model displays mass and speed. Extend it on paper to the instantaneous kinetic energy K(t) = m(t)v(t)^2/2 of the remaining rocket; this is not the energy of the rocket plus all expelled exhaust.
missions.prediction: Would K prime = mva include every change, or does the decreasing mass contribute another term?
missions.manipulate: Record m and v at 25%, 50% and 75% of the default burn. Keep mass in kilograms and speed in meters per second; the interface does not directly compute K or its derivative.
missions.decision: Derive K prime using product and chain rules. Then differentiate a(t) = ve q/m(t) using a quotient or negative power. Explain the role and sign of each mass derivative.
missions.clue: For constant positive q, m prime = -q. In a product, differentiate each factor in turn while leaving the other factors unchanged.

missions.title: Follow flow through mass into speed
missions.brief: One change travels through three linked quantities: time, remaining mass and speed.
missions.connection: The composition is t to m0 - qt to ve ln(m0/m). The mass decreases while speed increases, so the signs in the chain rule matter.
missions.prediction: At the same burn percentage, will doubling flow change speed, acceleration, both, or neither?
missions.manipulate: Fix dry mass 2000 kg, propellant 6000 kg and exhaust speed 3000 m/s. At 50% progress, compare flow 50 and 100 kg/s. Record time, remaining mass, speed and acceleration.
missions.decision: Derive dv/dt as (dv/dm)(dm/dt). Use those factors to explain the observations, and explain why equal burn percentages are not equal elapsed times when flow changes.
missions.clue: Treat m0 as fixed during one burn. Both dv/dm and dm/dt are negative; their product gives a positive acceleration.

missions.title: Find a tangent without solving the whole orbit
missions.brief: A circular path can be described by one equation even where it is not a graph y(x).
missions.connection: Choose a lunar circular orbit. Its center-relative coordinates satisfy x^2 + y^2 = r^2 with fixed r; implicit differentiation describes a local slope where such a slope is finite.
missions.prediction: At the rightmost point of the circle, will dy/dx be a finite number? How could the spacecraft still have a well-defined velocity?
missions.manipulate: Set lunar altitude 100 km, press Circular, and move from the starting point to a quarter orbit. Compare the directions of position and velocity. Use the center radius, not altitude, in the circle equation.
missions.decision: Differentiate the circle equation locally and identify where solving for dy/dx is valid. At the exceptional points, use the parametric velocity direction to explain the vertical tangent without dividing by zero.
missions.clue: When y depends on x, the derivative of y^2 is 2y times dy/dx. A vertical tangent can have a valid parametric direction even when its slope is undefined.

missions.title: Finish a burn quickly within an acceleration limit
missions.brief: The fastest allowed burn must obey the acceleration limit throughout its entire duration.
missions.connection: Fix dry mass M = 2000 kg, propellant P = 6000 kg and exhaust speed ve = 3000 m/s. Choose constant flow q in the allowed range to minimize burn time P/q while acceleration never exceeds 150 m/s^2.
missions.prediction: Will the acceleration constraint be tightest at ignition, halfway through, or just before cutoff?
missions.manipulate: Compare flow 50, 100 and 150 kg/s at the beginning and at 100% progress. The 100% acceleration is the left-hand limit immediately before the engine switches off.
missions.decision: Derive the feasible flow interval and choose the flow with the shortest burn time. Justify why checking the final pre-cutoff acceleration controls every earlier instant.
missions.clue: Remaining mass decreases to M, so the largest burning acceleration is ve q/M. Burn time decreases as positive q increases; the constraint can determine the optimum endpoint.

missions.title: Separate orbital speed from radial speed
missions.brief: A spacecraft can move quickly while its distance from the Moon is momentarily unchanged.
missions.connection: For center-relative position (x,y), let r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2). Differentiating r^2 = x^2 + y^2 connects radial speed to the two velocity components.
missions.prediction: At the nearest and farthest points of an ellipse, does zero radial speed mean that the spacecraft stops?
missions.manipulate: Set a lunar altitude of 100 km and choose Ellipse. Compare the start, a quarter orbit and a half orbit, then compare with Circular. Watch altitude and velocity direction; arrow lengths are rescaled for display.
missions.decision: Derive r times dr/dt = x vx + y vy. Explain the signs of radial speed on outward and inward portions, and distinguish total speed from radial speed at the two turning points.
missions.clue: The radial rate is the projection of velocity along the radius. Altitude and center distance differ by a constant, so they have the same time derivative.

missions.title: Recover travel distance from a speed curve
missions.brief: The area under this ideal rocket speed curve measures how far it travels during the burn.
missions.connection: Speed is nonnegative throughout this straight burn, so displacement and distance both equal the integral of speed over elapsed time. A table allows an approximation before using an antiderivative.
missions.prediction: Will trapezoids overestimate or underestimate the distance under this upward-curving speed graph?
missions.manipulate: Use the default burn and the five table readings at 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100%. Form four trapezoids using actual times in seconds. Compare the total with the 100% distance readout, which is in kilometers.
missions.decision: Convert units, report the approximation error, and explain its sign from the curve shape. Add intermediate readings to test how refinement changes the estimate.
missions.clue: Each trapezoid contributes average endpoint speed times elapsed seconds. For a convex speed curve, its secant segment lies above the curve.

missions.title: Check that accumulated distance returns the speed
missions.brief: A total accumulated over time has a rate of change at the current instant.
missions.connection: Let x(t) = integral from 0 to t of v(s) ds. While remaining mass is positive, the speed formula is continuous, so the fundamental theorem connects this accumulated distance to current speed.
missions.prediction: Will a short-interval change in the distance readout approach the speed at the middle of that interval?
missions.manipulate: Use the default burn. Record distance at 49%, 50% and 51%, converting kilometers to meters and burn percentage to seconds. Compute a centered average rate of distance change.
missions.decision: Compare the estimate with v at 50%. State the continuity condition that justifies x prime = v, and explain why this does not say that total distance and current speed are the same quantity.
missions.clue: The integration variable s ranges over past times. The upper endpoint t changes, adding a thin strip of area whose area per second approaches v(t).

missions.title: Integrate a logarithmic burn curve
missions.brief: Substitution reveals a simpler variable, but a second technique is still needed to find distance.
missions.connection: The on-screen distance comes from integrating ve ln(m0/(m0 - qt)). Recreate that calculation on paper with remaining mass m = m0 - qt, then integration by parts.
missions.prediction: When you replace time with remaining mass, why do the bounds run downward even though elapsed time runs upward?
missions.manipulate: Record the 50% and 100% distance of the default burn. Use mass bounds from m0 to m(t), with dt = -dm/q; the interface does not perform your symbolic integration.
missions.decision: Derive a distance expression that is zero at t = 0, then check both readouts after converting meters to kilometers. Differentiate your expression to verify it returns the speed.
missions.clue: After substitution, integrate ln(m0/m). Integration by parts separates that logarithm from its derivative. Its argument must be the dimensionless ratio m0/m.

missions.title: Measure a signal over a whole cycle
missions.brief: Two signals can have different shapes but the same root mean square amplitude.
missions.connection: For one base period T, RMS = sqrt((1/T) integral of y(t)^2 dt). The signal combines a base sine with an integer harmonic; these are relative amplitudes, not measured sound pressure or loudness.
missions.prediction: With harmonic 2 and fixed mix, will changing its phase change the full-period RMS? Will your answer stay the same for harmonic 1?
missions.manipulate: Set base frequency 200 Hz, harmonic 2 and mix 0.5. Compare phases 0, 90 and 180 degrees, then repeat with harmonic 1. Read both the waveform and RMS.
missions.decision: Expand the squared sum inside the integral. Explain why the cross term averages to zero for distinct integer harmonics and why equal frequencies can reinforce or cancel instead.
missions.clue: Average over a whole base period. Integrals of products of distinct integer-frequency sines vanish over that period; a same-frequency cross term can depend on phase.

missions.title: Examine an impossible zero-mass endpoint
missions.brief: An unbounded speed does not automatically imply an infinite distance.
missions.connection: The live model always keeps positive dry mass. Extend its formula only on paper toward T = m0/q, where remaining mass approaches zero; that endpoint is outside the physical model.
missions.prediction: As v(t) grows without bound near this hypothetical T, must the area under the speed curve also diverge?
missions.manipulate: Compare dry masses 500 and 2000 kg with the other default parameters. Both burns stop at positive mass. Use these finite curves only as motivation for the separate limiting calculation.
missions.decision: Test the limit of the integral of v from 0 to b as b approaches T from below. Compare it with the integral of acceleration over the same interval, and distinguish a finite accumulated distance from bounded speed.
missions.clue: Use u = m0 - qt. A logarithmic singularity and a 1/u singularity have different integrability near u = 0; always write the endpoint limit explicitly.

missions.title: Refine a polygon around a circular flight
missions.brief: A sequence of straight-sided approximations can approach the length of a curved orbit.
missions.connection: Choose a circular orbit of center radius r. On paper, an inscribed regular N-gon has perimeter L_N = 2Nr sin(pi/N); the simulator shows the circle but does not vary this polygon count.
missions.prediction: Will increasing N produce perimeters above or below the circumference? Why should the gaps shrink?
missions.manipulate: Set lunar altitude 100 km and press Circular. Use the resulting center radius to compute L_N for N = 4, 8, 16 and 32. Sketch representative chords against the orbit.
missions.decision: Use the limit sin(u)/u as u approaches zero to establish the limit of L_N. Explain why a few improving numerical estimates suggest the answer but do not prove convergence.
missions.clue: Rewrite L_N as 2 pi r times sin(pi/N)/(pi/N). Use center radius, not the 100 km altitude, when computing lengths.

missions.title: Approximate the rocket logarithm with a series
missions.brief: Repeatedly adding simple terms can approximate the logarithm behind rocket speed.
missions.connection: If z is consumed propellant divided by initial total mass, then v/ve = -ln(1-z). For 0 <= z < 1, its series is z + z^2/2 + z^3/3 + ...; the live model evaluates the logarithm directly.
missions.prediction: Will four terms be equally accurate early and late in a burn? Will a positive-term partial sum overestimate or underestimate speed?
missions.manipulate: Use the default rocket at 25%, 50% and 75%. Compute z from consumed mass, then compare one-, two- and four-term approximations with the speed readout.
missions.decision: State the convergence range used here and justify the error direction. Give a bound for the omitted positive tail using a geometric series; explain why z = 1 requires a separate divergence argument.
missions.clue: Beyond the Nth term, replace every denominator by N+1 to bound the remaining sum above. A burn percentage is not z because the rocket also contains dry mass.

missions.title: Approximate the beginning of a sound wave
missions.brief: A short polynomial can imitate a sine wave near one phase, without describing the whole cycle.
missions.connection: Set mix to zero. With phase variable u = 2 pi f t, the first cubic Taylor approximation is sin(u) approximately u - u^3/6; the polynomial calculation happens on paper.
missions.prediction: If frequency doubles, will a fixed accuracy window in phase correspond to the same time window or half as much time?
missions.manipulate: Use frequency 100 Hz and mix 0. Convert u = 0.2, 0.5 and 1 radian to times using t = u/(2 pi f), then compare sin(u) with the cubic. Repeat the time conversion at 200 Hz; the graph labels time in milliseconds.
missions.decision: Bound the error for these positive u <= 1 using the next alternating-series term. Choose a time range for a stated error tolerance, without claiming the local cubic is accurate across an entire period.
missions.clue: The omitted next term has magnitude u^5/120. A phase bound becomes a time bound only after dividing by 2 pi f and checking seconds versus milliseconds.

missions.title: Resolve motion into radial and sideways parts
missions.brief: Position and velocity point in different directions and answer different questions about a flight.
missions.connection: For planar position r = (x,y) and velocity v = (vx,vy), r dot v measures outward or inward motion after division by |r|. Embedding both in three dimensions also gives a signed angular-momentum direction from r cross v.
missions.prediction: Will r dot v be positive throughout an ellipse? What should it be on a circular orbit?
missions.manipulate: Choose a lunar Ellipse at altitude 100 km. Compare outward, farthest and inward portions, then compare Circular. Read velocity components; arrow lengths are rescaled. For numerical cross-products on the ellipse, use the start and half-orbit, where y = 0 and x is the closest radius or minus the farthest radius.
missions.decision: Classify the sign of r dot v in each region and explain the zero cases. Compute x vy - y vx at the two ellipse endpoints just specified, using the radius and velocity readouts, and connect its sign to the direction of travel.
missions.clue: A dot product detects the component along another vector. In this plane the cross product points along the z axis; a positive value corresponds to counterclockwise motion.

missions.title: Distinguish a flat image from a tilted object
missions.brief: The same two-dimensional outline can come from different three-dimensional arrangements.
missions.connection: This portal is strictly two dimensional. A vertical scale of 0.5 can also match the xy projection of a flat object rotated 60 degrees about the x axis in three dimensions; the missing depth is not rendered.
missions.prediction: Does an object appearing half as tall prove that its actual three-dimensional height or length was halved?
missions.manipulate: Set x scale 1, y scale 0.5, angle 0 and pan 0. On paper compare (x,y,0) mapped to (x,0.5y,0) with the rigid rotation (x,0.5y,(sqrt(3)/2)y).
missions.decision: Explain why both constructions have the same xy projection but preserve different three-dimensional lengths. Identify an additional view or depth measurement that would distinguish them.
missions.clue: Projection discards a coordinate. In the rigid rotation, the squared y and z components still add to y^2; the flat scaling has no compensating depth component.

missions.title: Change one rocket parameter at a time
missions.brief: A design sensitivity only has meaning when you specify what stays fixed.
missions.connection: The final ideal speed is F(M,P,ve) = ve ln(1+P/M), with positive dry mass M, nonnegative propellant P and fixed exhaust speed ve during a burn.
missions.prediction: Will adding propellant and adding dry mass change final speed in the same direction? Can raw output changes be compared if the input steps differ?
missions.manipulate: At 100% progress start from M = 2000 kg, P = 6000 kg and ve = 3000 m/s. Add one 250 kg propellant step, reset, then add one 100 kg dry-mass step. Also test one exhaust-speed step.
missions.decision: Derive the three partial derivatives and their units. Divide each measured output change by its own input change, then use a linear approximation to predict a small combined change and check it.
missions.clue: In a partial derivative, freeze the other design variables. Differentiate the ratio P/M carefully: varying P is not the same operation as varying M.

missions.title: Transport area through a portal
missions.brief: A coordinate transformation changes the area element as well as each point.
missions.connection: For the linear portal A = R(theta) diag(sx,sy), the Jacobian determinant is sx sy. Extend the visual to a double integral of unit density over a transformed region; the interface does not evaluate arbitrary integrals.
missions.prediction: Will a negative scale make area negative? Will rotation or horizontal translation change the total area?
missions.manipulate: Use x scale 2 and y scale 0.5, then negate x scale. Change angle and pan while observing the shape and determinant. Finally set one scale to zero.
missions.decision: Write the change-of-variables area formula with the absolute determinant. Explain orientation reversal, area preservation for these nonzero scales, and why collapse at zero scale is not an invertible change of variables.
missions.clue: Signed determinant records orientation; absolute determinant gives area scaling. A zero determinant maps a two-dimensional region into a lower-dimensional set.

missions.title: Read gravity as a field, not a path tangent
missions.brief: A gravity vector points toward the center even while the spacecraft moves sideways.
missions.connection: The exterior point-mass field is g(r) = -mu r/|r|^3 for r nonzero. The model samples it along one planar trajectory; it does not show the whole three-dimensional field.
missions.prediction: On a circular orbit, should gravity point along velocity or across it? How should its magnitude change when center distance increases?
missions.manipulate: Choose lunar altitude 100 km and press Circular. Record the field direction and acceleration magnitude. Repeat at altitude 1000 km, pressing Circular again after the altitude change.
missions.decision: Compare the magnitudes using the square of the ratio of center distances. Explain why g supplies acceleration r double-prime rather than velocity r prime, and identify the singular point excluded from the formula.
missions.clue: The vector numerator has length |r|, leaving field magnitude mu/|r|^2. Altitude must be increased by the Moon radius before using this inverse-square relationship.

missions.title: Compare gravity work with distance traveled
missions.brief: A spacecraft can travel a long closed path while gravity does zero net work over that cycle.
missions.connection: Specific work along a path is integral g dot dr. In the exterior central field, g = grad(mu/r), so endpoint radii determine the work; this is different from the arclength integral.
missions.prediction: For a complete noncolliding orbit, will positive distance traveled imply positive net gravity work?
missions.manipulate: Compare lunar Circular and Ellipse at starting altitude 100 km. Inspect the start, halfway point and completed orbit. Use center radii and speeds to compare mu(1/r_final - 1/r_initial) with the change in speed squared divided by two.
missions.decision: Explain the work sign on outward and inward legs and why the complete-cycle value is zero. Contrast that result with positive distance traveled, stating that the model does not evaluate arbitrary vector-field integrals.
missions.clue: A line integral of a gradient depends only on endpoint potential values. Keep orbit distances in kilometers and speeds in kilometers per second so specific work uses km^2/s^2.

missions.title: Extend a gravity circle to a spherical flux
missions.brief: The weakening field and the growing area of a sphere can exactly compensate.
missions.connection: The orbit panel is planar. On paper, extend the exterior point-mass field to a three-dimensional sphere centered on the body, with outward orientation and radius R outside its surface.
missions.prediction: If R doubles, what happens separately to gravitational field strength, sphere area and the total outward flux?
missions.manipulate: Use two lunar Circular presets at different altitudes to compare field magnitudes with center radius. Then calculate g dot n and integrate it over an imaginary sphere; that sphere is not rendered by the panel.
missions.decision: Derive the flux -4 pi mu and explain its negative sign. State why applying the divergence theorem to a point-mass field through a volume containing its singular origin requires care; use a shell excluding the origin instead.
missions.clue: On the sphere, g dot n = -mu/R^2 and area is 4 pi R^2. Zero divergence away from the origin does not permit ignoring a singularity inside a proposed volume.

missions.title: Build a portal displacement from two directions
missions.brief: Two transformed basis directions are enough to reconstruct every transformed displacement.
missions.connection: With pan zero, the portal is linear: A(a,b) = a A(1,0) + b A(0,1). The two displayed basis images explain the transformation without guessing from the sprite outline.
missions.prediction: Where should the displacement (2,-1) go if the first basis direction doubles and then both directions rotate 90 degrees?
missions.manipulate: Set pan 0, x scale 2, y scale 1 and angle 90 degrees. Read the two basis images and combine two copies of the first with minus one copy of the second. Repeat after negating x scale.
missions.decision: Show the vector calculation and check its direction against the portal. Then change pan and explain why a position shifts but the displacement between two transformed positions does not acquire that extra translation.
missions.clue: Write (2,-1) as 2(1,0) - (0,1). In a difference of two positions, the same added translation cancels.

missions.title: Read the columns of a portal
missions.brief: The order in which transformations act matters even when the same settings are used.
missions.connection: The live portal scales first and then rotates: A = R(theta) D, where D has the two scales on its diagonal. Its columns are the images of the standard basis vectors.
missions.prediction: Will scaling x by 2 and then rotating 90 degrees give the same matrix as doing those two operations in the opposite order?
missions.manipulate: Set pan 0, x scale 2, y scale 1 and angle 90 degrees, then compare with angle 0. Compute R D and D R on paper; the controls always implement scale then rotate, not an order switch.
missions.decision: Match the displayed basis images to the columns of R D. Give a vector for which the opposite-order matrix produces a different result, and explain the order using matrix multiplication.
missions.clue: The rightmost matrix acts first on a column vector. Multiplying a basis vector extracts the corresponding matrix column.

missions.title: Recover a point from its portal image
missions.brief: Inverting a transformation means solving for an input, and a collapsed dimension changes the possible answers.
missions.connection: For pan zero, finding the source of an image b means solving A x = b. When one scale becomes zero, some targets become impossible while others have many preimages.
missions.prediction: Will every target still have exactly one source after the vertical scale is set to zero?
missions.manipulate: Begin with x scale 2, y scale 1, angle 90 degrees and pan 0. Solve for the input whose image is (-3,4). Then set y scale 0 and inspect the collapsed range.
missions.decision: Use row operations to justify the first solution. For the collapsed matrix, choose one target with infinitely many preimages and one with none; identify the free variable or contradiction in each system.
missions.clue: With the second scale zero and this rotation, every image lies on the vertical axis. If pan is nonzero, subtract the translation from the target before solving the linear system.

missions.title: Tell a subspace from a shifted line
missions.brief: A straight image is not automatically a vector subspace.
missions.connection: A linear transformation has a kernel and an image that are subspaces. Adding a translation can shift its image away from the origin, producing an affine set instead.
missions.prediction: If the collapsed image is shifted one unit to the right, will it remain closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication?
missions.manipulate: Set x scale 2, y scale 0, angle 90 degrees and pan 0. Identify the image line and the inputs that map to zero. Now change pan to 1 and compare the translated line.
missions.decision: Give bases and dimensions for the kernel and image of the linear part. Explain why the shifted full-map image fails the subspace test, using a specific closure failure or the missing zero vector.
missions.clue: Every subspace contains zero and is closed under linear combinations. A translation changes positions but does not change the matrix of the underlying linear part.

missions.title: Find gains along unchanged lines
missions.brief: Some directions keep their line under a transformation even if they reverse direction.
missions.connection: An eigenvalue lambda satisfies A v = lambda v for a nonzero vector v. Negative eigenvalues reverse a direction; a real rotation need not have a real eigenvector.
missions.prediction: Which lines remain unchanged under horizontal scale 2 and vertical scale -1? What changes for a pure 90-degree rotation?
missions.manipulate: Use pan 0, angle 0, x scale 2 and y scale -1. Compare the two basis images. Then set both scales to 1 and angle to 90 degrees.
missions.decision: Find the eigenvalues from det(A - lambda I) for both matrices. Explain the absence of nonzero real eigenvectors for the quarter-turn, and distinguish the real-number problem from its complex eigenvalues.
missions.clue: An eigenvector needs a nontrivial solution of (A - lambda I)v = 0. Always specify the number field; complex roots do not create a visible real direction.

missions.title: Choose a direction for repeated stretching
missions.brief: Repeated applications reveal which components shrink and which grow.
missions.connection: With pan zero and angle zero, scales 1.5 and 0.5 give a diagonal matrix. Extend the single displayed transformation to repeated powers A^n on paper; the panel does not animate iteration.
missions.prediction: Starting from (1,1), will repeated transformations approach the horizontal direction, the vertical direction, or neither? Does approaching a direction mean approaching a finite point?
missions.manipulate: Set those scales and compare the two basis images. Calculate A^2(1,1) and A^4(1,1), then write the general expression using the eigenvector components.
missions.decision: Explain which eigenvector controls the normalized direction and what happens to the vector magnitude. Contrast this with a starting vector that has zero horizontal component.
missions.clue: Each eigenvector component is multiplied by its own eigenvalue on every step. Directional convergence and convergence of the vector itself are different statements.

missions.title: Test a routing claim before relying on it
missions.brief: A plausible shortcut rule can fail because it leaves out an important condition.
missions.connection: The invented network assigns each link a delay and the same independent failure probability. Hop count, total delay and success probability are three different route properties.
missions.prediction: Is the statement fewer hops implies less delay always true? Does fewer hops imply strictly higher success probability even when every link is perfectly reliable?
missions.manipulate: Set Ridge delay 4 ms and Crater delay 6 ms. Compare A-C-E with A-B-D-E. Compare their reliability first at failure 0%, then at 20%.
missions.decision: Give a counterexample to the delay implication. Rewrite the reliability claim with the conditions needed for a strict inequality, distinguishing a universal claim from an observation about one pair of routes.
missions.clue: One counterexample refutes an always statement. For common independent link-failure probability p, a k-hop route succeeds with probability (1-p)^k; p = 0 creates ties.

missions.title: Build route sets with clear membership rules
missions.brief: A route can belong to several useful categories at once.
missions.connection: Let R be all listed simple A-to-E routes, B the routes through Ridge, and F the routes with delay at most 12 ms. Complements must be taken relative to the stated universe R.
missions.prediction: If the Ridge link becomes slower, which of R, B and F can change?
missions.manipulate: Set Ridge delay 4 ms and Crater delay 6 ms. List B, F, their intersection, union and complements in R. Raise Ridge delay to 8 ms and repeat the membership checks.
missions.decision: Explain which sets stayed fixed and which changed. Test any claimed subset relation by checking every member rather than treating a shared member as proof of inclusion.
missions.clue: The sliders change weights, not which graph edges exist. A route set defined by topology can stay the same while a set defined by a delay threshold changes.

missions.title: Justify why a fastest route needs no loop
missions.brief: The route table omits repeated-vertex walks for a mathematical reason.
missions.connection: Every edge delay in this model is strictly positive. A shortest walk between two nodes cannot include a closed detour, because deleting that detour leaves a valid shorter walk.
missions.prediction: Could going around a loop ever improve total delay under these positive-edge assumptions?
missions.manipulate: Compare the listed routes at low and high adjustable delays. On paper, insert a closed detour into a route and calculate its extra cost; the interface lists simple routes rather than arbitrary looping walks.
missions.decision: Write a direct proof that every fastest walk in this model is simple. Identify exactly where positivity is used and explain why a few displayed examples alone cannot prove the general claim.
missions.clue: If a vertex repeats, remove the segment between two consecutive visits to that same vertex. Its positive total cost makes the remaining walk strictly shorter. Negative-edge models would require different reasoning.

missions.title: Count only routes the graph actually permits
missions.brief: A list of possible visits is not necessarily a valid path through the network.
missions.connection: A simple A-to-E route follows actual edges and never repeats a vertex. Split the count by the first step, A-B or A-C, then continue only through unused neighboring vertices.
missions.prediction: Would permuting the intermediate node names count the valid routes correctly, or would it include impossible paths?
missions.manipulate: Build a branching list by hand and compare each complete route with the table. Change the two adjustable delays and check whether the number of routes changes.
missions.decision: Give an exhaustive count with disjoint cases, explaining why no valid route was missed or counted twice. Distinguish counting routes from ranking them by delay.
missions.clue: Stop a branch when it reaches E. Do not add a step unless its edge exists and its next vertex has not already appeared in that route.

missions.title: Choose between fewest hops and least delay
missions.brief: A route can be shortest according to one definition and longer according to another.
missions.connection: This is a weighted undirected graph. An unweighted shortest path minimizes edge count; a weighted shortest path minimizes the sum of delays. The drawn geometric lengths are schematic.
missions.prediction: Will a minimum-hop route always be one of the fastest routes in this graph?
missions.manipulate: Begin with Ridge delay 4 ms and Crater delay 6 ms. Compare hop counts and delays, then raise each adjustable delay separately. At a tie, inspect all minimum-delay routes rather than only the highlighted one.
missions.decision: Choose a route for a strict latency objective and another for a minimum-hop objective. Explain any difference and state when more than one route is optimal.
missions.clue: First define the objective. Add the edge weights for latency; count edges for hops. Neither calculation uses the apparent length of a line on the drawing.

missions.title: Audit a shortest-route algorithm
missions.brief: A reliable route-finding procedure keeps global information instead of always taking the cheapest next edge.
missions.connection: The live table enumerates simple routes. Separately trace Dijkstra's algorithm on paper for this positive-weight graph, keeping tentative distances and a settled set.
missions.prediction: Why might greedily taking the cheapest edge from the current node fail to find the cheapest complete route?
missions.manipulate: Use Ridge delay 4 ms and Crater delay 6 ms. Starting at A, update tentative distances, settle the smallest unsettled distance and record predecessors. Repeat after changing one adjustable delay; compare the final E distance with the route table.
missions.decision: Explain the distinction between a locally cheapest-edge walk and Dijkstra's globally smallest tentative distance. State the nonnegative-weight assumption behind the settling argument and explain how the procedure terminates.
missions.clue: A relaxation asks whether a known route to one node plus the next edge improves another node's best known distance. A correct result in one example is a check, not a full correctness proof.

missions.title: Give route counting a probability model
missions.brief: Counting favorable routes gives a probability only after a route-selection rule is specified.
missions.connection: Imagine one equally likely ticket for each listed simple A-to-E route. This hypothetical uniform draw is separate from the interface, which deterministically highlights a fastest route.
