missions.prediction: Under that ticket rule, will changing a delay change the probability that the selected route passes through D?
missions.manipulate: At Ridge delay 4 ms and Crater delay 6 ms, count all listed routes and the routes containing D. Change Ridge delay while keeping every graph edge available and repeat the count.
missions.decision: Compute the probability and justify the equally likely denominator. Explain why the same route count would not determine a probability under an unspecified or fastest-route selection rule.
missions.clue: Probability by counting requires equally likely outcomes. Link failures use a different sample space; do not silently replace the route-ticket experiment with edge-failure patterns.

missions.title: Ask what a fast arrival tells you about its route
missions.brief: Conditioning changes the relevant group of possible outcomes.
missions.connection: Use a hypothetical uniform ticket draw from all listed routes. Let B mean the selected route includes Ridge and F mean its nominal delay is at most 12 ms; this concerns assigned delay, not conditioning on successful delivery.
missions.prediction: Will P(B given F) have the same denominator as P(B)? What if no route satisfies F?
missions.manipulate: With Ridge delay 4 ms and Crater delay 6 ms, list B, F and their intersection. Then increase Ridge delay to 8 ms and inspect whether F has any members.
missions.decision: Calculate the conditional probability when F is nonempty. Explain why the ordinary ratio definition is undefined when P(F) is zero, rather than assigning a value of zero.
missions.clue: Restrict the route tickets to F first. Among those remaining tickets, count the ones also in B; the conditioning group supplies the denominator.

missions.title: Infer which route a delivered packet used
missions.brief: A successful delivery can change your belief about a route that was selected before transmission.
missions.connection: Imagine choosing A-B-D-E or A-C-E with equal prior probability, then attempting one packet. Each link independently fails with the same probability; the live model supplies route success likelihoods, not this posterior.
missions.prediction: After learning that the packet arrived, should the two routes still have equal posterior probability?
missions.manipulate: Set link failure to 20% and compare the success probabilities of the three-hop and two-hop routes. Compute the posterior for the three-hop route, then repeat at failure 10% and 30%, keeping the equal prior rule fixed.
missions.decision: Normalize prior times likelihood and explain how the arrival evidence shifts the route probabilities. Distinguish this question from simultaneously sending copies along both routes, where shared links could create dependence.
missions.clue: The denominator is the sum of prior times success likelihood over the two mutually exclusive chosen routes. The posterior is not simply one route success probability.

missions.title: Turn a route draw into a delay value
missions.brief: Several different outcomes can produce the same numerical value.
missions.connection: For a hypothetical uniform draw from all listed simple routes, define X as the selected route nominal delay in milliseconds. The route is the outcome; its assigned delay is the random-variable value, whether or not a later delivery succeeds.
missions.prediction: If two routes have the same delay, do they become one equally likely outcome or contribute together to the probability of that value?
missions.manipulate: Use Ridge delay 4 ms and Crater delay 6 ms. Group route tickets by their delay. Repeat at Ridge delay 7 ms to create additional ties; the table itself remains deterministic.
missions.decision: Write the probability mass function of X and verify that its probabilities sum to one. Explain how changing weights can change this distribution while leaving the route sample space unchanged.
missions.clue: For each distinct delay value, add the probabilities of every route mapped to that value. Do not count distinct numerical values as equally likely without checking their multiplicities.

missions.title: Model a batch of packet deliveries
missions.brief: A batch distribution needs assumptions beyond a single-packet success probability.
missions.connection: Fix the three-hop route A-B-D-E and link failure 20%, giving per-packet success s = (1-0.2)^3. If packet attempts are also independent with this same s, the number delivered in n attempts is binomial.
missions.prediction: When attempts increase from 20 to 80, how will the expected count and the spread of the delivered fraction change?
missions.manipulate: Keep that route and failure setting, and compare packet counts 20 and 80. Use the row probabilities and expected counts; the model does not generate random delivery outcomes.
missions.decision: Write the binomial probability formula, mean and standard deviation. Compare spread for counts versus proportions and state when a normal approximation would be reasonable instead of assuming it always applies.
missions.clue: Independence of links within one attempt does not automatically imply independence between attempts. For the binomial model, both the per-packet success rate and the cross-packet assumptions must be stated.

missions.title: Choose a route for an average-delivery target
missions.brief: The fastest nominal route may not deliver the largest expected number of packets.
missions.connection: For n attempts and per-packet route success s, the expected delivered count is ns. This is a model average, not a guarantee about any particular batch.
missions.prediction: With link failure 20%, will the faster three-hop route or the slower two-hop route deliver more packets on average?
missions.manipulate: Set Ridge delay 4 ms, Crater delay 6 ms, failure 20% and packets 20. Compare A-B-D-E with A-C-E, then double the packet count while keeping the route probabilities unchanged.
missions.decision: Choose between those routes for a nominal delay limit of 14 ms and an expected-delivery target of at least 12 out of 20. Explain why a plan that meets this expectation could still miss 12 actual deliveries.
missions.clue: Add the expectations of the packet-success indicators. Linearity of expectation does not require cross-packet independence, although the displayed route probability uses independent link failures.

missions.title: Define whose route delay you are averaging
missions.brief: A sample can represent a stated population, but a convenient selection can answer a different question.
missions.connection: For this exercise, the finite population is every listed simple A-to-E route at fixed link settings, with each route counted once. It is not the population of real packets, which could use routes at unequal rates.
missions.prediction: Will the three fastest listed routes give a representative estimate of the mean delay across all routes?
missions.manipulate: Fix Ridge delay 4 ms and Crater delay 6 ms. Compute the full route-population mean, then the mean of the three fastest routes. Describe a simple random sample of three distinct route tickets without replacement.
missions.decision: Compare the convenient selection with the proposed random design. Specify the population, sampling units and target mean, and explain why changing the link settings creates a different population of delay values.
missions.clue: Every three-route subset must be equally likely in a simple random sample without replacement. A fastest-first rule systematically favors lower delays; the table does not perform a random sample for you.

missions.title: Separate an estimate from a known population value
missions.brief: An estimator can be unbiased over repeated samples even when a particular sample misses the target.
missions.connection: Keep a fixed finite population of listed route delays, each route weighted equally. Imagine selecting three distinct routes by simple random sampling without replacement; the complete table lets you compare an estimate with the true population mean.
missions.prediction: If a random sample mean is below the population mean, does that single outcome prove the estimator is biased?
missions.manipulate: At Ridge delay 4 ms and Crater delay 6 ms, calculate the population mean and the means for several three-route subsets. Imagine a fresh random selection from the full ticket set for each repetition, not repeated slider changes.
missions.decision: Explain why the sample mean is unbiased under the stated design and why its realized error need not be zero. Describe how sampling without replacement changes variability compared with independent draws with replacement.
missions.clue: Bias concerns the mean of an estimator over the sampling design. Equal inclusion probabilities make each population value contribute equally on average; finite-population correction reduces variability when sampling a substantial fraction.

missions.title: Test a delivery claim using supplied trial data
missions.brief: A model claim and a hypothetical observed batch play different roles in a test.
missions.connection: Fix route A-B-D-E. The null claim is independent identical packet success probability s = (1-0.2)^3. Use the supplied hypothetical observation of 6 deliveries in 20 attempts; this count was not produced by the simulator.
missions.prediction: If the alternative is worse reliability, which outcomes should count as at least as unfavorable to the null as 6 deliveries?
missions.manipulate: Set failure 20% and packets 20 to read the null expected count. On paper compute the lower-tail binomial probability P(X <= 6) for n = 20 and s = 0.8^3. Choose a significance level before making the decision.
missions.decision: State the null, alternative, p-value and decision at your chosen level. Explain why the p-value is not the probability that the null is true, and why correlated packet failures would require another model.
missions.clue: Compute probabilities assuming the null, then add the probabilities of the observed outcome and more extreme outcomes in the direction specified by the alternative.

missions.title: Notice when a routing rule bends a data pattern
missions.brief: A changing optimal route can turn a simple input-output relationship into a piecewise one.
missions.connection: Use a deliberately chosen design grid: Crater delay fixed at 6 ms and Ridge delay varied. These deterministic model outputs are not a random observational sample or a noisy experiment.
missions.prediction: Will fastest-route delay keep increasing at the same rate as Ridge delay becomes large, or can the routing choice create a plateau?
missions.manipulate: Record fastest-route delay at Ridge settings 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 ms. Fit a line through the first three observations, then calculate its residuals for all five. Inspect which routes are optimal at each setting.
missions.decision: Compare a single straight-line description with a piecewise rule that accounts for a route switch. Explain why a good descriptive fit here supplies neither real-world causal evidence nor inferential p-values without an additional data-generating model.
missions.clue: For these settings compare the route cost Ridge + 6 with the fixed competing cost 13. A minimum of two expressions can bend even when each expression is linear.

missions.title: Shrink uncertainty without changing an observed rate
missions.brief: The same sample proportion can support different precision when sample sizes differ.
missions.connection: Imagine independent identical packet trials on a fixed route with an unknown success probability. Use supplied hypothetical observations 15 of 25 and 60 of 100; neither count is generated by the model.
missions.prediction: Both samples have proportion 0.6. If sample size quadruples, how should an approximate confidence interval width change?
missions.manipulate: Fix route A-B-D-E and failure 20%, then compare packet settings 25 and 100. Treat the shown expected counts only as model outputs. Separately calculate intervals from the two supplied observed counts.
missions.decision: Compare the approximate 95% intervals p-hat plus or minus 1.96 sqrt(p-hat(1-p-hat)/n). State the independence and large-count assumptions, and explain 95% coverage as a property of repeated interval construction, not a probability attached to a fixed unknown parameter.
missions.clue: At fixed p-hat the standard-error estimate is proportional to 1/sqrt(n). This normal interval is approximate, particularly for small samples or proportions near the boundaries; dependence can change its coverage.

missions.title: Choose evidence for a network reliability claim
missions.brief: A simulation based on assumed reliability cannot independently verify that assumption.
missions.connection: The route success readouts follow specified independent-link probabilities. A claim about actual network delivery requires observed outcomes and a sampling or experimental design beyond this synthetic graph.
missions.prediction: Would reading the same expected-delivery value repeatedly create additional evidence that a real network meets a reliability target?
missions.manipulate: Compare the fixed routes A-B-D-E and A-C-E while holding link failure and packet count constant. Identify which results are deterministic consequences of the assumptions, then outline a separate real-data collection plan.
missions.decision: Define the target quantity, trial unit, outcomes and conditions to record. Propose random selection of trial times or randomized route assignment where appropriate, account for shared disturbances, and state what the planned data could and could not justify.
missions.clue: Separate an assumed probability, a model prediction and an observed relative frequency. Shared failures can make packets dependent; more simulated expected values do not substitute for independent observations.

missions.title: Make the water promise precise
missions.brief: Turn “enough for everyone” into a claim with a stated universe and a testable negation.
missions.connection: The manifest computes one allowed crew plan. On paper, distinguish evidence from one plan from a statement about every allowed plan.
missions.prediction: Is “six tanks hold enough water for every allowed crew plan” true? What exactly would one counterexample need to show?
missions.manipulate: Set 3 people, 4 days, and 2.5 L per person per day. Then change only the crew to 4 people. Compare the required liters with the 30 L capacity of six tanks.
missions.decision: Let D be the set of plans allowed by the controls and V(p) their water need. Write the claim as “for every p in D, V(p) ≤ 30” and write its exact negation. Use a model setting to justify your verdict. Explain why one successful plan would not prove the universal claim.
missions.clue: Negating “for every” produces “there exists.” Keep the same universe and negate the inequality; do not merely replace “every” with “some.”

missions.title: Prove that one fewer tank cannot work
missions.brief: A packing rule deserves a proof of both sufficiency and minimality.
missions.connection: Whole-tank packing gives a concrete ceiling function. The model supplies examples; your proof must cover every positive required volume, not only those examples.
missions.prediction: For V > 0 liters and 5 L tanks, does n = ceiling(V/5) merely work, or is it the smallest possible tank count?
missions.manipulate: Set 3 people, 3 days, and 3.5 L per person per day to require 31.5 L. Compare the displayed seven tanks with the 30 L capacity of six. Try an exact multiple of 5 L as well.
missions.decision: Prove 5n ≥ V, then prove every nonnegative integer m < n has 5m < V. State where integrality is used. Include the exact-multiple case, where rounding adds no extra tank.
missions.clue: The defining ceiling inequalities are n − 1 < V/5 ≤ n. A smaller integer is at most n − 1; a smaller real number need not be.

missions.title: Decide whether the portal can be undone
missions.brief: An inverse requires each output to identify exactly one input.
missions.connection: The portal displays an affine function T(p) = Ap + b. On paper, analyze injectivity and surjectivity on the full plane, including the zero-scale case.
missions.prediction: Does moving the origin with a horizontal translation destroy invertibility, or does a zero scale cause the real problem?
missions.manipulate: Keep the rotation at 0°, vertical scale at 1, and translation at 1. Compare horizontal scale 2 with horizontal scale 0. Observe the sprite and basis direction that collapses.
missions.decision: For T(x,y) = (2x + 1,y), give a formula for the inverse and verify both compositions. For T(x,y) = (1,y), exhibit distinct inputs with the same output and one output in R² that is never reached.
missions.clue: Undo the translation before dividing by a nonzero scale. A map can still be a function when it has no inverse function.

missions.title: Locate a threshold that rounding cannot define
missions.brief: Use completeness to define an escape threshold between bound and unbound motion.
missions.connection: The orbit model illustrates the energy sign. The least-upper-bound argument is a written statement about real speeds; a rounded slider value cannot certify exact equality.
missions.prediction: At a fixed radius, can a finite list of tested bound speeds identify the greatest bound speed?
missions.manipulate: Choose Lunar spacecraft at 100 km altitude. Compare speeds 2 and 3 km/s and read the energy classification and escape-speed readout. Keep the starting radius fixed.
missions.decision: Let S = {v in [2,3] : v² < 2μ/r₀}, with μ = 4902.800118 km³/s² and r₀ = 1837.4 km. Show S is nonempty and bounded above. Identify sup S, decide whether it belongs to S, and explain what completeness contributes.
missions.clue: The supremum is √(2μ/r₀), but the strict inequality excludes that speed from S. A set may have a least upper bound without a largest element.

missions.title: Make shrinking time intervals precise
missions.brief: A rate at one instant is the limit of rates over nonzero intervals.
missions.connection: The burn model gives the reference velocity curve. A written sequence of difference quotients lets you justify the limit beyond the slider’s finite time resolution.
missions.prediction: With the default burn, will a forward average acceleration starting at t = 30 s be above or below the instantaneous acceleration there?
missions.manipulate: Use dry mass 2000 kg, propellant 6000 kg, flow 100 kg/s, and exhaust speed 3000 m/s. Read the states at 50%, 75%, and 100% of the burn; relate these to t = 30, 45, and 60 s.
missions.decision: Define hₙ = 30/n seconds and aₙ = [v(30 + hₙ) − v(30)]/hₙ, where v(t) = 3000 ln(8000/(8000 − 100t)). Justify aₙ → 60 m/s² and why each finite-n quotient is larger. State the time and positive-mass domain.
missions.clue: Use the mean value theorem on each interval. The acceleration 300000/(8000 − 100t) is continuous and increasing while mass stays positive. Never set hₙ to zero inside the quotient.

missions.title: Separate a continuous map from a usable inverse
missions.brief: A smoothly changing portal can still lose the information needed to undo it.
missions.connection: Changing horizontal scale makes a continuous family of maps. The epsilon–delta statement and the failure of a continuous inverse at zero belong in your written analysis.
missions.prediction: As horizontal scale s approaches zero, do the transformed points jump? Does the inverse remain well behaved?
missions.manipulate: Set angle and translation to 0 and vertical scale to 1. Move horizontal scale through 1, 0.1, 0, and −0.1. Follow the blue basis direction and the invertibility readout.
missions.decision: For the image f(s) = (s,0) of the unit x-vector, prove continuity at every s₀ using the Euclidean norm and find f′(s₀). Then explain why undoing the map requires division by s and why this inverse cannot extend through s = 0.
missions.clue: Here ‖f(s) − f(s₀)‖ = |s − s₀|, so δ = ε works. Continuity of the forward map does not prevent its determinant from becoming zero.

missions.title: Justify the area used in an energy budget
missions.brief: A smooth daylight curve has an integral even before numerical rectangles are chosen.
missions.connection: The stage model integrates solar production separately from its stepped battery dispatch. On paper, justify the production integral using upper and lower sums.
missions.prediction: Does doubling peak production double the day’s generated energy? Must it also double energy actually served to the load?
missions.manipulate: Keep load and battery fixed and compare peaks 0, 4, and 8 kW. Read generated, spilled, and unserved energy separately; do not treat these as the same quantity.
missions.decision: For peak 4 kW, prove P(t) = 4 sin(π(t−6)/12) on [6,18] is Riemann integrable, then find its integral in kWh. Explain why continuity makes the upper-minus-lower sum tend to zero and why battery clipping can break proportionality for served energy.
missions.clue: The production integral is 96/π kWh. On daytime, |P′| ≤ π/3 kW per hour, so a uniform partition with mesh Δt has upper-minus-lower sum at most 12(π/3)Δt.

missions.title: Keep a small waveform error from hiding a large slope error
missions.brief: Uniformly small changes in a signal need not give uniformly small changes in its derivative.
missions.connection: The two-tone controls show a few members of a sequence. The infinite sequence and its uniform bounds must be analyzed on paper, beyond the available harmonic settings.
missions.prediction: If a second tone’s amplitude tends to zero while its frequency grows, must the derivative error also tend to zero?
missions.manipulate: Use f = 220 Hz and phase 0°. Compare harmonic 2 with amplitude 0.5 and harmonic 4 with amplitude 0.25. Notice the smaller added wave but faster oscillation.
missions.decision: For gₙ(t) = sin(2πft) + sin(2πnft)/n on [0,1/f], prove uniform convergence to sin(2πft). Differentiate and show why gₙ′ does not converge uniformly to the derivative of that limit. Contrast this with keeping harmonic 2 fixed while its amplitude becomes 1/n.
missions.clue: The waveform error is at most 1/n. In the growing-frequency case the derivative error is 2πf cos(2πnft), whose supremum stays 2πf.

missions.title: Test whether a portal has one complex derivative
missions.brief: Complex differentiability requires the same quotient limit from every direction.
missions.connection: The portal can show real linear maps of the complex plane. Complex difference quotients and the Cauchy–Riemann test are written extensions, not a built-in complex solver.
missions.prediction: Will stretching x by 2 and y by 1 have the same derivative when approached along real and imaginary increments?
missions.manipulate: Set angle and translation to 0. Compare scales (2,1) with scales (2,2). Then rotate the equal-scale portal by 30° and observe that it still scales every direction equally.
missions.decision: Identify z = x + iy. For F(z) = 2x + iy, compute the difference quotient along real increments and along imaginary increments. For G(z) = 2e^(iπ/6)z, prove a single complex derivative exists everywhere. State why nonzero derivative matters if you also claim angle preservation.
missions.clue: For F, the two quotients are 2 and 1. For G, cancellation leaves 2e^(iπ/6) for every nonzero complex increment; equal scaling plus rotation is complex multiplication.

missions.title: Integrate around a loop without filling its hole
missions.brief: The inside of a closed path matters when the integrand has a singularity.
missions.connection: A circular orbit supplies a geometric loop around the origin. The complex integrals are paper calculations, not gravitational work computed by the orbit model.
missions.prediction: Should both ∮z dz and ∮(1/z) dz vanish on the same counterclockwise circle?
missions.manipulate: Choose Lunar spacecraft, then Circular. Move through a complete path and note its orientation and that it surrounds the origin without passing through it.
missions.decision: Parameterize the loop by z(θ) = r e^(iθ), 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, with fixed r > 0. Compute both contour integrals. Explain why a theorem requiring holomorphy throughout the enclosed disk applies to z but not to 1/z.
missions.clue: Use dz = ir e^(iθ)dθ. The second integrand simplifies to i dθ, so its integral is 2πi; being defined on the path is not the same as being holomorphic inside it.

missions.title: Check where a series is allowed to follow the path
missions.brief: A power series can fail on a contour even though the contour integral itself is well defined.
missions.connection: Normalize the model’s circular path to the unit circle on paper. The model shows the contour; it does not plot poles or evaluate residues.
missions.prediction: If a pole moves from a = 1.5 to a = 0.5 on the real axis, can the same power-series expansion about zero still be used on |z| = 1?
missions.manipulate: Select Circular and follow the full counterclockwise loop. Sketch a normalized unit circle and mark the two proposed pole locations on your own diagram.
missions.decision: For F(z) = 1/(z−a), derive the series −Σ zⁿ/aⁿ⁺¹ and its convergence radius. For each positive real a above, decide whether that series reaches the unit circle and compute ∮F(z)dz using the pole’s location. Explain why neither case puts a pole on the contour.
missions.clue: The radius is |a|. The residue at z = a is 1, so the counterclockwise integral is 2πi when a = 0.5 and 0 when a = 1.5.

missions.title: Build a reversible set of portal commands
missions.brief: The four quarter-turns form a group under composition.
missions.connection: The camera gives visible representatives of four rotations. The composition table and group axioms are paper tasks; the full set of scale controls is not this four-element group.
missions.prediction: If you apply two quarter-turn commands, must their composition remain one of the four commands?
missions.manipulate: Set both scales to 1 and translation to 0. Compare rotations 0°, 90°, 180°, and −90°; the last represents 270°.
missions.decision: Label the commands by 0,1,2,3 quarter-turns. Write their composition table modulo 4, identify the identity and each inverse, and justify associativity. Explain why allowing zero-scale commands would obstruct a group of reversible transformations.
missions.clue: Composition adds turn counts modulo 4. Associativity follows from function composition, not from how convincing one sequence of pictures looks.

missions.title: Find why matrix cancellation can fail
missions.brief: Nonzero matrices can multiply to the zero matrix.
missions.connection: The portal can display two diagonal projection matrices. Ring multiplication, addition, and the cancellation argument are written extensions in the ring of integer 2×2 matrices.
missions.prediction: Can two nonzero linear maps have a zero composition?
missions.manipulate: At angle 0° and translation 0, display P = diag(1,0) and then Q = diag(0,1). Notice which coordinate survives each projection.
missions.decision: Compute PQ and QP on paper, verify that neither P nor Q is zero, and use P·Q = P·0 to show why cancelling a nonzero matrix factor is invalid here. Explain which extra property, invertibility, would make left cancellation valid.
missions.clue: Q keeps only the vertical coordinate; P then discards it. Nonzero and invertible are different conditions in a matrix ring.

missions.title: Choose arithmetic that permits division
missions.brief: Undoing a nonzero scale illustrates the inverse property that field arithmetic requires.
missions.connection: Real scaling in the portal supplies the analogy. Arithmetic modulo 7 and modulo 6 is a paper extension; the camera still uses real coordinates.
missions.prediction: Can “divide by 2” mean multiplying by an inverse in every arithmetic system?
missions.manipulate: Set angle and translation to 0 and both scales to 2. Compare with both scales 0.5, and verify on paper that composing the two maps restores every vector. Also inspect zero scale.
missions.decision: Find the multiplicative inverse of 2 modulo 7, then prove that 2 has no inverse modulo 6. Explain why the nonzero residues modulo a prime form the multiplicative part of a field, while the zero scale has no inverse even over R.
missions.clue: Modulo 7, 2·4 ≡ 1. Modulo 6, every multiple of 2 is even, so it cannot be congruent to 1; 2·3 ≡ 0 is also a zero-divisor warning.

missions.title: Choose a bundle size that fits two manifests
missions.brief: The greatest common divisor finds the largest equal bundle with no leftovers.
missions.connection: The manifest gives integer tank counts. The Euclidean algorithm and the proof that a bundle size divides both counts are written work.
missions.prediction: If two trips need six and eight tanks, is four tanks per bundle possible for both trips?
missions.manipulate: At 4 days and 2.5 L per person per day, compare crews of 3 and 4. Confirm the required six and eight 5 L tanks.
missions.decision: Use the Euclidean algorithm to find the largest positive integer number of tanks per bundle that divides both manifests. Prove why the algorithm’s remainder step preserves the common divisors, and report the bundle counts for each trip.
missions.clue: From 8 = 1·6 + 2, every common divisor of 8 and 6 divides 2, and every common divisor of 6 and 2 divides 8. A two-tank bundle gives three and four bundles.

missions.title: Time a message for a repeating receive window
missions.brief: Equal clock phases need not mean equal travel times.
missions.connection: The network supplies route delays. A receiver that opens every 7 ms is a written scheduling extension; the model does not simulate that clock.
missions.prediction: For a 10 ms route, would sending at phase 0 make the message arrive when the 7 ms clock reads 0?
missions.manipulate: Keep Base–Ridge at 4 ms and Crater–Relay at 6 ms. Add the delays along A–B–D–E, then change Base–Ridge to 8 ms and recompute that same route even if another route becomes faster.
missions.decision: Solve t + 10 ≡ 0 (mod 7) for a departure phase t in {0,…,6}. Compare with the 14 ms route after the change. Explain why two arrival times with the same residue can still be different elapsed times.
missions.clue: Reduce the delay first: 10 ≡ 3 (mod 7), so t ≡ 4. Congruence describes phase, while latency remains measured in milliseconds.

missions.title: Combine two tank sizes exactly
missions.brief: An integer constraint changes a continuous-looking packing equation.
missions.connection: The model supplies a 45 L demand using 5 L tanks. Introducing 8 L tanks is a written extension; the live model continues to use only 5 L tanks.
missions.prediction: If partial tanks and leftover capacity are disallowed, can every real solution of 5a + 8b = 45 be used as a manifest?
missions.manipulate: Set 3 people, 6 days, and 2.5 L per person per day. Confirm 45 L and the nine-tank baseline before considering a second tank size on paper.
missions.decision: Find every nonnegative integer solution to 5a + 8b = 45, where a and b count 5 L and 8 L tanks. Choose the solution using the fewest tanks and prove that no five-tank solution could hold 45 L.
missions.clue: Modulo 5, b must be a multiple of 5. With 0 ≤ b ≤ 5, the options are (a,b) = (9,0) and (1,5). Five tanks hold at most 40 L.

missions.title: Verify a burn from its rate equations
missions.brief: The changing mass and acceleration determine the entire ideal burn.
missions.connection: The rocket model evaluates a closed-form solution of the burn ODEs. Verify that solution and its initial conditions before trusting the curve.
missions.prediction: With the same initial and final masses, does doubling fuel flow double the final ideal change in velocity?
missions.manipulate: Keep dry mass 2000 kg, propellant 6000 kg, and exhaust speed 3000 m/s. Compare flows 50 and 100 kg/s, moving each to 100% burn. Compare burn duration and final velocity separately.
missions.decision: Starting with m′ = −q and v′ = vₑq/m, derive m(t) = m₀−qt and v(t) = vₑ ln(m₀/m(t)) for v(0) = 0. Give the valid time interval and explain why flow changes burn duration but cancels from the final delta-v. State what changes when the engine stops.
missions.clue: Keep m(t) ≥ dry mass > 0 during the burn. The acceleration at 100% in this model is the limit immediately before shutoff; the burn equation must not be continued after fuel is gone.

missions.title: Give a vibrating string both space and time
missions.brief: A time waveform becomes a wave-equation solution only after spatial motion and boundary conditions are supplied.
missions.connection: The tone model shows temporal harmonics. A string displacement u(x,t) and its spatial derivatives are a written extension; no string or PDE solver is hidden in the plot.
missions.prediction: Can a single sound trace tell you the displacement at every point of a string?
missions.manipulate: Use base frequency f = 220 Hz, harmonic 2, amplitude b = 0.5, and phase 0°. Compare the two components and their sum.
missions.decision: On paper set L = 1 m, c = 2Lf, and u(x,t) = sin(πx/L)sin(2πft) + b sin(2πx/L)sin(4πft). Verify u_tt = c²u_xx and u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0. Show that at x = L/3 this displacement is √3/2 times the model waveform.
missions.clue: Differentiate each mode twice in space and time. The relation 2πf = cπ/L makes the coefficients agree; the end conditions come from the spatial sine factors.

missions.title: Give portal calibration one global minimum
missions.brief: A squared calibration error can be certified convex rather than judged by appearance.
missions.connection: The portal shows the transformed basis directions. The objective and its convexity proof are written work; the controls do not run an optimizer.
missions.prediction: Can averaging two poorly calibrated scale settings produce a better setting than either endpoint?
missions.manipulate: Set angle and translation to 0. Compare scales (2,0), (0,2), and their midpoint (1,1). Use the unchanged original shape as the target.
missions.decision: For F(a,b) = (a−1)² + (b−1)², compute the endpoint and midpoint errors. Prove convexity on R² and show that (1,1) is the unique global minimizer, not merely a locally good slider setting.
missions.clue: The Hessian is 2I, which is positive definite. Alternatively, expand the error at a convex combination and identify the subtracted term λ(1−λ)‖u−v‖².

missions.title: Distinguish a stationary tone from a quiet tone
missions.brief: A zero derivative can mark either a maximum or a minimum.
missions.connection: Equal-frequency interference gives a periodic objective. Treat phase as a real variable in the written optimization; the model displays one 0°–360° period.
missions.prediction: At zero phase the waveform is stationary with respect to a tiny phase change. Does that make it the quietest combination?
missions.manipulate: Set harmonic 1 and second amplitude 1. Compare phases 0°, 180°, and 360°, keeping the base frequency fixed. Read RMS as well as the waveform.
missions.decision: Using phase φ in radians, minimize J(φ) = RMS² = 1 + cos φ over all real φ. Find every stationary point and classify it. Explain why optimizing the squared RMS avoids the square-root corner at complete cancellation.
missions.clue: J′(φ) = −sin φ and J″(φ) = −cos φ. Odd multiples of π give the global minimum 0; even multiples give the global maximum 2.

missions.title: Keep the payload requirement inside the optimization
missions.brief: The best mathematical answer must satisfy the mission’s mass constraint.
missions.connection: The burn model evaluates candidate masses. Enforcing the payload requirement and proving the best feasible choice are written optimization tasks.
missions.prediction: If total starting mass stays 8000 kg, should the greatest ideal delta-v occur at an interior split between dry mass and fuel?
missions.manipulate: Keep exhaust speed 3000 m/s and flow 100 kg/s. Compare (dry mass, propellant) = (2000,6000), (4000,4000), and (6000,2000) kg at the end of each burn.
missions.decision: Maximize Δv = 3000 ln(8000/d) subject to d + p = 8000, d ≥ 2000, and p ≥ 0. Identify the active constraint at the optimum and give a monotonicity proof. Explain why a 500 kg dry-mass setting, though available in the model, is infeasible for this specified mission.
missions.clue: After eliminating p, the feasible interval is 2000 ≤ d ≤ 8000 and the derivative is −3000/d. There is no interior stationary point to find.

missions.title: Protect a tiny velocity change from cancellation
missions.brief: Equivalent formulas can behave differently in finite-precision arithmetic.
missions.connection: The rocket uses a stable logarithm calculation internally. The slider illustrates small fuel use; a much smaller fuel fraction u = 10⁻¹² is a paper numerical-analysis case beyond its control resolution.
missions.prediction: When used fuel is a tiny fraction of starting mass, could subtracting nearly equal numbers erase meaningful digits?
missions.manipulate: Use 2000 kg dry mass, 250 kg propellant, and 1% burn. Compute u = fuel used / initial mass and compare the velocity with the first-order estimate vₑu.
missions.decision: Compare −vₑ ln(1−u) with the mathematically equivalent −vₑ log1p(−u). Explain where rounding in 1−u causes loss of relative accuracy for very small u. Use −ln(1−u) = u + u²/2 + … to estimate the absolute error of vₑu for 0 < u < 1.
missions.clue: The leading neglected term is vₑu²/2, and the full positive tail is at most vₑu²/[2(1−u)]. A stable formula reduces rounding error; it does not remove approximation error.

missions.title: Solve the hidden angle in an orbit clock
missions.brief: Position on an ellipse requires solving an equation, not moving uniformly around the drawn curve.
missions.connection: The model solves Kepler’s equation with bisection. Work through one bracket yourself to connect a solver’s stopping rule with its angle error.
missions.prediction: At one quarter of an elliptical orbit’s period, must the eccentric anomaly also be exactly π/2?
missions.manipulate: Select Lunar spacecraft, then Ellipse, and move time to 25%. This preset has eccentricity e = 0.3225. Compare the equal-time dots with the geometry of the path.
missions.decision: For M = π/2, solve F(E) = E − 0.3225 sin E − M = 0 by bisection on [π/2,π]. Prove a unique root exists there and find how many interval halvings guarantee that the midpoint error is below 0.0001 rad.
missions.clue: F′(E) ≥ 1−e > 0. After n halvings the bracket width is (π/2)/2ⁿ and its midpoint error is at most half that width; thirteen halvings suffice.

missions.title: Check a quadrature rule against known solar energy
missions.brief: An exact reference separates integration error from battery-dispatch error.
missions.connection: The model integrates solar production exactly but dispatches storage in small time steps. Your trapezoidal calculation is an independent paper approximation of the solar integral.
missions.prediction: For the concave-down daylight arch, will straight-line trapezoids overestimate or underestimate generated energy?
missions.manipulate: Set peak production to 4 kW and read generated energy. Keep that value as the reference while you mark daylight samples at 6, 9, 12, 15, and 18 hours on paper.
missions.decision: Use four equal trapezoids to approximate the daytime integral. Compare 12 + 12√2 kWh with the exact 96/π kWh. Then bound the trapezoidal error using max|P″| = π²/36 and state why a mismatch in battery storage is a different numerical issue.
missions.clue: For interval length 12 h and step 3 h, the composite trapezoidal error bound is (12)(3²)(π²/36)/12 = π²/4 kWh. An error bound need not equal the actual error.

missions.title: Keep a numerical burn inside its physical interval
missions.brief: Time steps must respect both error and the event that changes the equations.
missions.connection: The model’s closed-form burn is a reference curve. Euler time stepping is a written extension; changing the progress slider does not change the solver’s step size.
missions.prediction: Will forward Euler underestimate or overestimate velocity during a burn whose acceleration increases with time?
missions.manipulate: Use the default 60 s burn. Read velocity and mass at 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% to compare with your computed time steps.
missions.decision: Starting from m₀ = 8000 kg and v₀ = 0, apply mₖ₊₁ = mₖ − 100h and vₖ₊₁ = vₖ + h·300000/mₖ with h = 30 s, then h = 15 s, stopping at 60 s. Compare both with 3000 ln 4 m/s. Explain why a step beyond burnout must switch equations.
missions.clue: For h = 30 s the velocity estimate is 2925 m/s, below the exact value. Each left-endpoint acceleration is too small for its interval; dry mass must never be consumed as fuel.

missions.title: Tell continuity from an open-image property
missions.brief: Collapsing a dimension can be continuous even when it sends an open disk to a thin line.
missions.connection: The portal supplies a concrete map between Euclidean metric spaces. Neighborhoods, preimages, and open-set proofs are written extensions.
missions.prediction: Does a continuous function have to send every open set to an open set?
missions.manipulate: At zero rotation and translation, compare scales (2,1) with (0,1). Observe that points move continuously as the horizontal scale shrinks, while the image loses a dimension at zero.
missions.decision: Prove T(x,y) = (2x,y) is continuous using ‖T(p)−T(q)‖ ≤ 2‖p−q‖. For Q(x,y) = (0,y), explain why continuity still holds but the image of an open unit disk is not open in R². Keep the codomain topology explicit.
missions.clue: Continuity concerns preimages of open sets. The vertical interval produced by Q is open in the vertical line’s subspace topology, but not in the whole plane.

missions.title: Guarantee that the burn reaches a target speed
missions.brief: A continuous image of a compact connected time interval cannot have a missing middle speed.
missions.connection: The model visualizes velocity on a closed burn interval. Compactness, the intermediate value theorem, and what changes for an open interval require written justification.
missions.prediction: Could the ideal burn go continuously from 0 to more than 4000 m/s while never reaching 2000 m/s?
missions.manipulate: Use the default masses and exhaust speed. Compare the start, middle, and end of the 60 s burn, then find approximately where the velocity crosses 2000 m/s.
missions.decision: Explain why v([0,60]) is compact and connected. Use the closed-form velocity to establish that 2000 m/s occurs exactly once. Then replace the domain by (0,60) and state which endpoint values are no longer attained and why compactness is lost.
missions.clue: The mass remains at least 2000 kg, so v is continuous throughout [0,60] and strictly increasing. Solve t = 80(1−e^(−2/3)) s for the target; continuity supplies existence and monotonicity supplies uniqueness.

missions.title: Join the two ends of a phase control
missions.brief: A phase is a point on a circle even when its control is drawn as a line segment.
missions.connection: The tone model makes 0° and 360° produce the same signal. The quotient topology and a two-phase product space must be described on paper; only one relative phase is adjustable here.
missions.prediction: Do phase values near 0° and near 360° represent far-apart sounds just because their displayed numbers are far apart?
missions.manipulate: Fix frequency, harmonic, and amplitude. Compare phases 0°, 5°, 355°, and 360°. Observe the agreement at the endpoints and the small changes across the wrap.
missions.decision: Describe [0,360] with its endpoints identified and explain why it models a circle rather than a closed interval. If both oscillator phases were independently adjustable modulo 360°, identify the product parameter space and explain why a square would need both pairs of opposite edges identified.
missions.clue: Use the map φ ↦ (cos φ, sin φ), with degrees converted to radians. Two independent circular phases give S¹ × S¹, a torus; the current control shows only one circular coordinate.

missions.title: Measure bending independently of speed
missions.brief: Curvature describes a path’s geometry, while speed describes how quickly it is traversed.
missions.connection: The circular orbit supports a curvature calculation for a planar curve. Surface curvature is not computed by this model; derive the curve formula from position, velocity, and acceleration on paper.
missions.prediction: If two objects traverse the same circle at different speeds, must the circle have different curvature?
missions.manipulate: Choose Circular at 100 km altitude, then choose Circular again at 1000 km altitude. Compare the radii and circular speeds. Use the numerical quantities rather than arrow lengths, which are rescaled for display.
missions.decision: For a regular planar curve derive κ = |vₓaᵧ−vᵧaₓ|/|v|³ and apply it to a circle of radius r to get 1/r. Compare the two model curvatures in km⁻¹. Distinguish changing the time parameter from changing the gravitational speed needed to maintain that orbit.
missions.clue: For circular motion, acceleration has magnitude v²/r and is perpendicular to velocity. The powers of v cancel in the curvature formula; the orbital radius is lunar radius plus altitude.

missions.title: Cover a circular path with usable coordinates
missions.brief: One coordinate can fail even though the path remains perfectly smooth.
missions.connection: The model supplies points and tangents on a circle. An atlas of local charts and transition maps is a written construction, not an extra coordinate-chart widget.
missions.prediction: Can the x-coordinate alone label every point of a circle uniquely?
missions.manipulate: Choose Circular and inspect time 0%, 25%, 50%, and 75%. Compare locations sharing the same x-coordinate and note the changing tangent direction.
missions.decision: Construct four charts using the open right, left, upper, and lower semicircles. On the right chart, use y as coordinate and recover x = √(r²−y²) for |y| < r; write the analogous inverse maps. Explain why these charts cover the circle and why their overlap maps are smooth.
missions.clue: Projection onto x fails to distinguish upper and lower points. A chart needs a locally one-to-one coordinate and a smooth inverse; switching charts avoids the square-root endpoint where that inverse derivative fails.

missions.title: Distinguish a shortest surface route from a chord
missions.brief: The space in which a route must stay determines what “straight” and “shortest” mean.
missions.connection: The orbit display provides a central-angle picture. Travel on a spherical lunar surface is a paper extension; the spacecraft path is not a simulated surface geodesic.
missions.prediction: For two surface locations separated by 90° at the Moon’s center, can the straight chord through the interior be a usable surface route?
missions.manipulate: Select Circular and compare positions one quarter-turn apart to visualize the central angle. On a separate sphere diagram use lunar radius R = 1737.4 km, not the spacecraft’s larger orbital radius.
missions.decision: Find the minor great-circle distance and the chord length for that angle, stating their units and constraints. Explain why a great circle can have nonzero ambient acceleration while having zero intrinsic geodesic acceleration. What changes about shortest-path uniqueness for antipodal endpoints?
missions.clue: The surface arc is πR/2, while the chord is √2R. A great circle’s acceleration is normal to the sphere; antipodal points admit multiple shortest great-circle arcs of length πR.

missions.title: Measure hours rather than count plotted dots
missions.brief: Duration assigns a size to a set of times, including nonempty sets with zero duration.
missions.connection: The production curve shows when a threshold is exceeded. Lebesgue measure on the time interval and a sigma-algebra of events are written extensions; plotted sample counts are not the measure.
missions.prediction: Can the set containing only noon be nonempty and still have zero total duration?
missions.manipulate: Set peak production to 4 kW and load to 2 kW. Find the two times at which the solar arch meets the load line, then identify the interval strictly above it.
missions.decision: On Ω = [0,24] hours with its Borel sigma-algebra and Lebesgue measure, find the measure of A = {t : P(t) > 2 kW} and of {12}. If a time is chosen uniformly from the day, convert the first duration into a probability and state the normalization.
missions.clue: P(t) > 2 corresponds to 8 < t < 16, so the duration is 8 h and the uniform-time probability is 8/24. A singleton has measure zero without being empty.

missions.title: Turn quantized power readings into an integral
missions.brief: Simple functions can approach an analog production curve without changing the meaning of total energy.
missions.connection: The stage model gives the continuous reference power. Downward quantization and a sequence of simple functions are paper extensions, not editable sensor data in the simulator.
missions.prediction: If every reading is rounded down more finely, must the estimated generated energy increase toward the analog value?
missions.manipulate: Set peak production to 4 kW and note the daytime arch and the generated total. On paper, round selected power values down to steps of 1 kW, 0.5 kW, and 0.25 kW.
missions.decision: For the numerical power P(t) in kW, define Pₙ(t) = 2⁻ⁿ floor(2ⁿP(t)) on [0,24], with n ≥ 0. Prove these are nonnegative measurable simple functions increasing pointwise to P. Apply monotone convergence and bound the missing energy by 24·2⁻ⁿ kWh.
missions.clue: Each finer grid keeps the previous lower reading or raises it by half its old step. Since 0 ≤ P−Pₙ < 2⁻ⁿ, the total error has an explicit bound as well as a convergence theorem.

missions.title: Choose the norm that matches signal error
missions.brief: A small average-square error and a small worst-case error are different requirements.
missions.connection: The model displays a tone and its total RMS. Norms of the difference from the base tone are calculated on paper; total signal RMS is not automatically the error norm.
missions.prediction: With a second-harmonic amplitude of 0.5, will the maximum error from the base tone equal the RMS error?
missions.manipulate: Set harmonic 2 and phase 0°. Compare amplitudes 0, 0.5, and 1. Normalize time by u = ft so one base period becomes [0,1].
missions.decision: For the added error e(u) = b sin(4πu), compute ‖e‖∞ and ‖e‖₂ on [0,1] with Lebesgue measure. Evaluate both at b = 0.5. Explain why changing a function at only one time does not change its L² equivalence class, even though a pointwise value changed.
missions.clue: The worst-case error is |b| and the L² error is |b|/√2. In Lp spaces with p < ∞, functions equal almost everywhere represent the same element.

missions.title: Model a relay that remembers an outage
missions.brief: Independent failures and persistent up/down states require different probability models.
missions.connection: The network uses independent edge failures per packet. A relay with memory is a written Markov-chain extension; changing the failure slider does not install that chain in the simulator.
missions.prediction: If a relay failed on the previous transmission, must its chance of working next time still be the independent model’s 90%?
missions.manipulate: Set failure to 10% and inspect the route success probabilities. Identify the independence assumption before replacing it on paper with state-dependent transitions.
missions.decision: Use states Up and Down and row-stochastic matrix P = [[0.9,0.1],[0.4,0.6]]. Starting Up, calculate the probability of being Up after two steps. Find the stationary row distribution π with πP = π and explain why positive transition probabilities ensure convergence to it.
missions.clue: The two-step Up probability is 0.9² + 0.1·0.4 = 0.85. Balance π_Up·0.1 = π_Down·0.4 with probabilities summing to 1; the stationary Up probability is 0.8.

missions.title: Separate packet counts from arrival rates
missions.brief: A mean rate does not by itself specify how random arrivals are spaced.
missions.connection: The network computes reliability for a chosen packet count. Poisson arrival times, waiting times, and thinning are paper extensions; the model does not generate a timeline or queue.
missions.prediction: If messages arrive at an average of two per second, must exactly six arrive in every three-second window?
missions.manipulate: With failure 10%, use the default A–B–D–E route of three edges and set packets sent to 6. Compare its expected deliveries with six guaranteed arrivals.
missions.decision: Assume arrivals form a Poisson process of rate 2 s⁻¹ and packet deliveries are mutually independent with probability q = 0.9³, independent of arrivals. Find the three-second arrival mean, probability of no arrivals, mean interarrival time, and mean delivered count. Explain why a fixed half-second renewal schedule has the same rate but a different arrival law.
missions.clue: The arrival mean is 6, zero-arrival probability is e⁻⁶, and mean waiting time is 0.5 s. Independent thinning gives delivery rate 2q = 1.458 s⁻¹ and a three-second delivery mean of 4.374.

missions.title: Remove predictable drift from a packet count
missions.brief: A fair fluctuation process is obtained by subtracting conditional expected growth.
missions.connection: The network gives an expected count, not a random sample path. Martingale reasoning and the distinction from Brownian motion must be developed on paper.
missions.prediction: Is a growing delivery count itself a martingale when every new packet has a positive chance of arriving?
missions.manipulate: Keep the default three-edge route and failure 10%. Compare expected delivered counts for 10 and 20 packets; use q = 0.9³ for each independent packet.
missions.decision: Let Xₖ be independent Bernoulli(q) delivery indicators, Sₙ = X₁ + … + Xₙ, and Fₙ the history of the first n outcomes. Prove Mₙ = Sₙ−nq is an integrable martingale with respect to Fₙ. Explain why these discrete jumps are not literally a Brownian path even though both centered models can have mean-zero increments.
missions.clue: Independence gives E[Xₙ₊₁ | Fₙ] = q, so E[Mₙ₊₁ | Fₙ] = Mₙ. Brownian motion has continuous paths and Gaussian increments; the packet indicators are discrete and bounded.

missions.title: Give an infinite tone expansion a place to converge
missions.brief: A complete function space makes sense of a Cauchy sequence of increasingly rich signals.
missions.connection: Two visible harmonics introduce an inner-product geometry. Infinite sums and completeness of L²([0,1]) require written reasoning; the model contains only two components.
missions.prediction: Can observing the first two harmonics prove that every future partial sum converges?
missions.manipulate: Set harmonic 2, amplitude 0.5, and phase 0°. With normalized time u = ft, this is the first two terms of s_N(u) = Σ from n=1 to N of 2^(1−n) sin(2πnu).
missions.decision: Use orthogonality to express ‖s_M−s_N‖₂² for M > N, then show the sequence is Cauchy. State where completeness of the Hilbert space L²([0,1]) guarantees a limit. Also bound the pointwise tail by the geometric sum to explain why this particular series converges uniformly.
missions.clue: The squared L² tail is (1/2)Σ from n=N+1 to M of 4^(1−n), while the absolute infinite tail is at most 2^(1−N). Verifying this series is not a proof that every normed function space is complete.

missions.title: Measure one tone with a linear functional
missions.brief: A frequency measurement can be a bounded linear map from a function space to a number.
missions.connection: The two components make a base-tone measurement tangible. The integral functional and its continuity proof are paper analysis, not an additional frequency analyzer in the model.
missions.prediction: If only a second harmonic is added, must a measurement of the first harmonic’s coefficient change?
missions.manipulate: Set harmonic 2 and phase 0°, then compare second amplitudes 0 and 1. Notice that the total RMS changes while the base component keeps the same amplitude.
missions.decision: On real L²([0,1]), define L(g) = 2∫₀¹g(u)sin(2πu) du. Prove linearity and |L(g)| ≤ √2‖g‖₂, then evaluate it for g(u) = sin(2πu) + b sin(4πu). Explain why point evaluation at u = 0 is not even well defined on L² equivalence classes.
missions.clue: Cauchy–Schwarz uses ‖sin(2πu)‖₂ = 1/√2; orthogonality removes the second harmonic. Two representatives can differ at one point while defining the same L² element.

missions.title: Separate the sound a projection keeps from what it rejects
missions.brief: A projection has distinct spectral roles for its range and its kernel.
missions.connection: The model separates two harmonics visually. The operator below acts on an entire Hilbert space and is analyzed on paper; the simulator does not run arbitrary spectral decompositions.
missions.prediction: If a filter keeps only the base sine component, should applying that same ideal filter twice change anything further?
missions.manipulate: Use harmonic 2, phase 0°, and amplitude 0.5. Identify the base sine and the added second sine before imagining that the second component is removed.
missions.decision: On real L²([0,1]), let Pg = 2(∫₀¹g(u)sin(2πu) du)sin(2πu). Prove P² = P, show P is bounded and self-adjoint, and identify its eigenvalue-1 space and eigenvalue-0 space. Explain why its spectrum is {0,1}, considering its complexification if using the complex definition of spectrum.
missions.clue: The range is the span of sin(2πu), and the kernel is its orthogonal complement. Every g splits as Pg + (I−P)g; for λ other than 0 or 1, invert P−λI separately on those two subspaces.
